### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Boles (2026) is now the best available national, school-level, course-by-course map of where AP STEM coursework was authorized in U.S. public high schools in 2015–2019, and the field should read it as exactly that: a verified descriptive landscape, not an adjusted-effect study. Its descriptive spine is unusually trustworthy. The College Board audit file covers the full population of 21,139 public high schools with non-offering schools added back, and every figure the sub-reviews recomputed from Tables 1 and 3 — roughly forty numbers across national rates, locale shares, and disproportionality gaps — reproduces to the decimal. The core facts need no modeling and can be cited with confidence: 48.0% of rural high schools obtained no AP STEM authorization in any of four years versus 20.9% of suburban schools; rural schools are 37.7% of high schools but 20.7% of those offering four or more courses; the deficit widens monotonically with the course-count threshold; and, unadjusted, rural and town schools trail on every one of the twelve courses, least in AP Calculus AB, Biology, and Chemistry. The caveats attach precisely to the paper's most quotable material. The headline that suburban schools offer 'nearly three times as many' AP STEM courses as rural schools (5.35 vs. 1.81) sits inside the adjusted-analysis section and is labeled as controlled, but three sub-reviews independently showed it cannot be a covariate-adjusted contrast — the implied structural-zero probabilities contradict the Model B coefficients it is attributed to, and it is in substance the raw locale gap. The size-adjusted count gap is about 14%, or roughly 0.8 courses. The school-size result — adding enrollment flips the sign of every locale coefficient in the zero-inflation model — is real and the paper's strongest analytic finding, but enrollment is partly constitutive of rurality rather than a confounder of it, so Model B decomposes the gap rather than dissolving it, and the widely quotable 'rural schools are 28.8% more likely to offer AP Calculus AB' is a product of that conditioning in a region of the covariate space where rural and suburban schools barely overlap. The abstract overstates the per-course result (Calculus AB reverses under controls and four courses show negligible adjusted gaps; the honest count is about eight of twelve, not eleven) and omits the size finding entirely; the by-course severity ranking holds on the odds scale but roughly reverses on the percentage-point scale; the AP Physics C: E&M column that carries the largest headline gap shows signs of quasi-separation; and the GWLR maps behind the fifth headline finding rest on estimates the paper deliberately withholds. Full reproduction is not possible from the published record — no code, no covariate descriptives, no audit-to-NCES crosswalk, no definition of the school universe (which appears to differ from prior national estimates: 66.7% of city schools offering an AP STEM course here versus the 88% the paper itself quotes from Mann et al.) — though the printed tables leave the descriptive claims fully auditable. Bottom line for the field: cite the tables, not the abstract; quote the unadjusted gaps as the policy-relevant facts and the adjusted ones as mechanism evidence about scale; treat the numbers as a pre-pandemic, pre-AP-Precalculus baseline; and watch for the audit-to-enrollment validation and finer rurality measures the paper plainly sets up.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The "11 of the 12 courses" sentence is on p. 19, in the Discussion, not in the abstract, and the criticism of it is withdrawn. Eleven of the twelve rural and town point estimates in Table 4 are negative, and p. 6 states that significance tests and standard errors are "not particularly useful" for full-population data, so by the paper's own standard the count is right. If significance is applied anyway, eight or nine of the estimates are distinguishable from zero; that is a caveat for readers, not an error in the paper. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

#### Key Strengths

- Population coverage with a verifiable descriptive core: all 21,139 U.S. public high schools, the full College Board audit file for 2015–2019, non-offering schools added back so the denominator is the whole population — and every descriptive number in the prose reproduces exactly from Tables 1 and 3, which is rare enough to materially raise trust in the tables.
- The course-by-course disaggregation (Table 3 unadjusted, Table 4 with state fixed effects and school controls) is, as far as any sub-reviewer could determine, the first national school-level estimate for all twelve AP STEM subjects, and it yields the paper's most useful novel finding: locale gaps are subject-specific — smallest in core-adjacent courses, largest in calculus-based physics, Calculus BC, and Computer Science A — with city schools leading on CS Principles and Environmental Science.
- The Model A / Model B contrast in Table 2 confronts the school-size-versus-rurality confound head-on rather than assuming it away, and the sign flip on all three locale coefficients in the zero-inflation component is a clean, informative decomposition of where the extensive-margin locale gap comes from.
- The spatial layer does real work: rural schools in CT, DE, MD, MA, and NJ show a county median of four or more AP STEM courses while rural schools in 23 states have a median of zero, which establishes that 'rural' is not one condition and earns the paper's well-argued critique of NCES locale codes in the limitations section.
- Reporting transparency is above field norms in several respects — software down to package versions, full coefficient tables with standard errors, AIC/BIC and Brier scores, an explicit statement that inference is not the point with population data, a candid audit-versus-enrollment limitation, and a deposited openICPSR data-access guide for the restricted College Board file.

#### Key Concerns

- The paper's most quotable number is not the estimand it is labeled as. The combined ZIP predictions (suburb 5.35, city 3.64, town 2.41, rural 1.81) imply structural-zero probabilities of roughly .09/.36/.51/.64 that flatly contradict Model B's zero-inflation coefficients, under which rural schools of a given size have lower odds of a structural zero than suburban schools. These are locale-specific marginal predictions that track the raw Table 1 gap; the genuinely adjusted count gap is about 14% (0.8 courses). Expect 'nearly three times as many, controlling for school characteristics' to be cited, and do not repeat it.
- School size is treated as a confounder but is closer to a mediator of rurality. Model B answers 'do rural schools trail suburban schools of the same enrollment?' (no — on the extensive margin they do slightly better), which is a mechanism finding, not the policy-relevant contrast, and 'school size accounts for much of the relationship' is not licensed by comparing raw coefficients across two logit-link models (noncollapsibility, no decomposition, no locale × size interaction, no common-support diagnostic). The rural AP Calculus AB 'advantage' (+28.8% odds against an unadjusted 37.9% vs. 72.8%) is an extrapolation produced entirely by this conditioning.
- The abstract and the prose outrun the tables in specific, quotable places: the abstract's 'likelihood of offering each course' is contradicted by Calculus AB; '11 of the 12 courses' is really about eight, since Biology, Chemistry (rural), and CS Principles show negligible adjusted gaps and town Calculus AB and city CS Principles are within two standard errors of zero; the 'high-math-demand' category is never enumerated and footnote 10's definition sweeps in Calculus AB and Statistics while excluding CS A; the severity ranking is an odds-scale artifact that reverses on the percentage-point scale (Statistics, Chemistry, and Biology have the largest rural–suburban point gaps; the physics C courses the smallest); and Figures 2 and 8 carry x-axis labels describing a quantity they do not plot.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The "11 of the 12 courses" sentence is on p. 19, in the Discussion, not in the abstract, and the criticism of it is withdrawn. Eleven of the twelve rural and town point estimates in Table 4 are negative, and p. 6 states that significance tests and standard errors are "not particularly useful" for full-population data, so by the paper's own standard the count is right. If significance is applied anyway, eight or nine of the estimates are distinguishable from zero; that is a caveat for readers, not an error in the paper. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

- Two parts of the modeling should be quoted only directionally. The AP Physics C: E&M logit — the column carrying the paper's largest headline gap — has an intercept of −25.9 and a log(proportion Asian) standard error ten times its neighbors, the signature of quasi-separation on the state fixed effects. The GWLR analysis behind the fifth headline finding reports no coefficients, bandwidth, kernel, or uncertainty (footnote 4), drops the state fixed effects used everywhere else (footnote 12), and yet supports state-specific claims about Iowa, South Carolina, New York, Vermont, and Maine that no reader can check. The 'structural zero' / 'no capacity' language throughout reifies a latent mixture class as a measured school attribute.
- The analysis cannot be rebuilt from the published record even with data access: no code in any form; no descriptive statistics for any covariate (so none of the predicted counts can be regenerated); an undocumented audit-to-NCES crosswalk whose unmatched records would land in the zero category that anchors the size finding; an undefined school universe (the 66.7% city rate in Table 1 versus the 88% the paper quotes from Mann et al. 2017 signals a materially different denominator); unreported constants inside the log transformations; an unexplained identical N across fourteen models; and no robustness checks — not even the twelve-category locale codes the paper holds and argues should matter.

#### What to Rely On

- The unadjusted locale gaps in AP STEM availability, 2015–2019 (Table 1): 79.1% of suburban, 66.7% of city, 63.3% of town, and 48.0% of rural public high schools obtained at least one AP STEM authorization; 7,982 schools (37.8%), 4,141 of them rural, obtained none in any of four years. These are population counts, verified to reproduce, and require no modeling.
- Rural underrepresentation widens with breadth: rural schools are 37.7% of high schools but 20.7% of those offering four or more AP STEM courses and 15.5% of rural schools reach five or more versus 58.8% of suburban schools (Table 1, Figure 2).
- Every AP STEM course is offered by a smaller share of rural and town schools than suburban schools unadjusted (Table 3), with the smallest relative rural deficits in Calculus AB, Biology, and Chemistry and the largest suburban overrepresentation in Physics C: E&M (+29.4 points of composition share), Physics C: Mechanics (+26.6), Physics 2 (+24.7), CS A (+23.7), and Calculus BC (+22.4) (Figure 8) — cite these as composition-share disproportionalities, not as gaps in offering rates.
- Locale gaps are subject-specific rather than uniform, and the ordering on the adjusted odds scale (Table 4, Figure 9) is genuinely largest for Physics C: E&M, Calculus BC, Physics 2, Physics C: Mechanics, and CS A and smallest for Calculus AB, Biology, and Chemistry — provided the claim is stated on the odds scale and the E&M magnitudes are treated as approximate.
- School enrollment is the dominant school-level correlate of whether a school holds any AP STEM authorization, and adding it reverses the sign of all three locale coefficients in the zero-inflation model (Table 2, Model A → B: city .375 → −.038, rural .341 → −.363, town .019 → −.192) — cite this as a decomposition showing the extensive-margin locale gap operates through scale, not as evidence that the gap disappears.
- Conditional on having a program, rural and town schools offer about 14–16% fewer AP STEM courses than suburban schools with the same enrollment and sociodemographics, and city schools about 3% fewer (Table 2, Model B count component) — the paper's genuinely adjusted intensive-margin gap, roughly 0.8 of a course.
- Rurality has heterogeneous curricular implications by region: rural schools in CT, DE, MD, MA, and NJ have a county median of four or more AP STEM courses while rural schools in 23 states (three Southern, eight Midwestern, twelve Western) have a median of zero (Figure 4). This is a county-level descriptive, not a GWLR result, and supports the paper's argument that NCES locale codes obscure rural heterogeneity.
- The paper's arithmetic. Every percent change quoted from Tables 2 and 4 (45.5/40.6/1.9; 3.41/14.14/15.90; 28.8/17.8/14.0/21.1), every national offering rate, and every disproportionality figure recomputes correctly; the one slip is a label ('AP Physics C: Magnetism' for Mechanics, p. 13). Numbers pulled from this paper's tables can be trusted.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- 'Suburban schools offer more than twice as many AP STEM courses as town schools and nearly three times as many as rural schools' (p. 12) as an adjusted finding — the combined predictions are inconsistent with the Model B coefficients as a common-covariate contrast and are effectively the raw gap; cite Table 1 for the descriptive gap and the ~14% count-model contrast for the adjusted one.
- 'Rural schools have 28.8% higher odds of offering AP Calculus AB than suburban schools' — true only after conditioning on enrollment in a region with little rural–suburban overlap; unadjusted, 37.9% of rural versus 72.8% of suburban schools offer it. The defensible claim is that Calculus AB is the course where the rural deficit is proportionally smallest.
- 'Gaps are largest for high-math-demand courses' (abstract) — the category is never enumerated, footnote 10's definition includes Calculus AB (the reversed exception) and Statistics (mid-pack) while excluding CS A (in the largest-gap list), and the ranking holds only on the odds scale; on the percentage-point scale the largest rural–suburban deficits are Statistics (40.8 pp), Chemistry (37.6), and Biology (36.9), and the physics C courses are the smallest (13.4 and 20.9).
- 'Rural and town schools are still less likely to offer each AP STEM course, with the exception of AP Calculus AB' / '11 of the 12 courses' — Biology (rural −.024, town −.049), Chemistry (rural −.123), and CS Principles (rural −.134, town −.250) are indistinguishable from zero in Table 4, and the cited town Calculus AB (+17.8%) and city CS Principles (+14.0%) 'exceptions' are unstarred; read Figure 9's confidence intervals alongside every per-course sentence on pp. 14–15.

Eleven of the twelve rural and town point estimates in Table 4 are negative, and p. 6 states that significance tests and standard errors are "not particularly useful" for full-population data, so by the paper's own standard the count is right. If significance is applied anyway, eight or nine of the estimates are distinguishable from zero; that is a caveat for readers, not an error in the paper. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

- 'School size accounts for much of the relationship between locale and structural support' — a raw coefficient comparison across two logit-link models with no decomposition; the 'odds ratio nearly halves' framing describes a sign reversal (OR 1.41 → 0.70), and Model B's rural coefficient means rural schools of a given size are less likely to be structural zeros, a sentence the paper never writes.
- Any magnitude from the AP Physics C: E&M column of Table 4 (rural −.562, town −.905) — the −25.9 intercept and the tenfold-inflated Asian-proportion standard error indicate quasi-separation; the direction is plausible, the precision is not.
- The state-specific GWLR claims (Iowa, South Carolina, New York, Vermont, Maine; pp. 15, 18) and Figures 10–11 generally — no estimates, bandwidth, or uncertainty are reported and state fixed effects are dropped; read as hypothesis-generating cartography.
- 'No structural support,' 'no capacity for AP STEM courses,' and 'schools with capacity' — labels for a latent ZIP mixture class identified by functional form alone; nothing in the data measures capacity, IB/DE reliance, or AP-program absence, and the audit file could have validated this (non-STEM AP audits with zero STEM audits) but was not used to.
- This paper's percentages placed next to other national AP-availability figures (Mann et al. 2017, Malkus 2016, NCES 2009) — the 21,139-school universe is never defined and appears to include alternative, virtual, and special-purpose schools that other estimates exclude (66.7% of city schools with an AP STEM course here versus the 88% quoted from Mann et al. on p. 5, in a measure that should be more generous, not less).
- Figures 2 and 8 — both x-axes say 'Percent of U.S. Public High Schools' but plot each locale's share of the course-offering subset; within-locale offering rates are in Tables 1 and 3, not in these figures. Figures 6 and 7 do not share a value domain despite the text saying the gradient is identical.
- The predicted course counts (5.869; 5.35/3.64/2.41/1.81) and anything downstream of them (Figures 6–7 choropleths) — no covariate means or fixed-effect convention are reported, so they are unverifiable and it is unstated whether the maps show count-only or combined predictions.
- Current-day relevance, especially for computer science — AP CS Principles launched in 2016–17, so its rural deficit partly measures rollout; AP Precalculus, state CS mandates, and post-2020 virtual AP delivery all postdate the window. Treat this as a 2015–2019 baseline.
- The discussion's dismissal of online delivery (p. 19) — sourced to COVID emergency-remote-instruction studies rather than to designed online AP programs (Hart et al. 2023 and Mader et al. 2025, which the paper cites only as future work), and in tension with footnote 2's implication that externally delivered AP is credited to whichever school completes the audit.
- The outcome itself — 'authorized to use the AP label in any of four years' is neither point-in-time availability nor a course actually taught nor enrollment; the paper says so, and a four-year zero is strong evidence of unavailability, but positive counts overstate what any student experienced in any year.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

A carefully executed population-scale descriptive study whose raw counts and shares are arithmetically impeccable and whose central claim — rural and town high schools offered far fewer AP STEM courses in 2015–2019 — is firmly established by the unadjusted evidence. The regression layer is competently specified but carries several interpretive hazards: school size is treated as a confounder when it is arguably a mediator of rurality, the headline 'nearly three times' locale gap appears to be a marginal rather than a covariate-adjusted contrast, the by-course ranking of gap severity reverses on the absolute scale, and the GWLR maps are reported with no estimates, no state fixed effects, and no uncertainty.

**Strengths:**

- True population coverage of a hard-to-obtain restricted dataset: all College Board AP audit records 2015–2019 for U.S. public high schools joined to CCD/EDGE, N = 21,139, with non-offering schools explicitly added back so the denominator is the full school population rather than the set of AP-offering schools. This eliminates sampling error and the selection-into-AP problem that limits most prior work (Handwerk et al. 2008; Mann et al. 2017).
- Every descriptive figure I could recompute is exactly right. Table 1 percentages reproduce from the counts (3,826/7,967 = 48.02% rural; 4,101/5,186 = 79.08% suburban); Table 3 national rates reproduce (Calc AB 11,094/21,139 = 52.48%; Physics C: E&M 1,569/21,139 = 7.42%); and every Figure 8 disproportionality value reproduces to the second decimal (suburban Physics C: E&M share 846/1,569 = 53.92% minus 24.53% = +29.39%; rural Calc BC 885/5,223 = 16.94%, 37.69 − 16.94 = 20.75%). This is unusually clean and materially raises confidence in the descriptive layer.
- The zero-inflated model is a defensible response to a real feature of the data. Figure 1 shows ~8,000 schools at zero against a nearly flat distribution across 1–12; a plain Poisson would badly underpredict that mass, and the paper says so and cites the right source (Gelman & Hill, 2007).
- The paper is honest about its most important construct limitation. The Limitations section states plainly that 'audit data overestimates coursework availability,' and footnote 2 notes that students can sit an AP exam without their school holding the audit. The paper does not claim causality anywhere.
- Sensible use of state fixed effects in both the ZIP and the twelve logits, which absorbs the large state-policy variation (AP mandates, exam-fee waivers, statewide virtual programs) that would otherwise contaminate a national locale contrast.
- The author's own critique of NCES locale codes in the Limitations section is well argued and correctly identifies that the four-category scheme treats a wealthy exurban rural school like an isolated distressed one.

**Weaknesses:**

- The combined ZIP predictions that anchor the paper's most quotable claim do not appear to be covariate-adjusted. The reported combined counts (suburb 5.35, city 3.64, town 2.41, rural 1.81) imply structural-zero probabilities of pi = .088 suburban, .358 city, .512 town, .641 rural — which flatly contradicts the Model B zero-inflation coefficients they are supposedly built from (rural −.363, OR 0.696, i.e. rural schools have LOWER conditional odds of a structural zero than suburban). Enrollment-weighting the four combined predictions returns a national mean of 3.20 courses, consistent with these being locale-specific marginal means rather than contrasts at common covariate values. The count-only predictions, by contrast, are explicitly evaluated 'using the suburban means of the covariates' (p. 11) and are internally consistent (5.869 × e^-.152 = 5.041 ≈ 5.039). So the paper presents a ~14% adjusted gap and a ~3x gap side by side, both labeled as being 'with school sociodemographic and enrollment controls.' They are not the same estimand.
- School size is treated as a confounder but is closer to a mediator, and the paper's central Model A→B comparison inherits that. Rural schools are small in substantial part because they are rural; conditioning on sqrt(enrollment) estimates a controlled direct effect that requires no unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding — implausible when district wealth, STEM teacher supply, and isolation drive both size and offerings. Model B's rural zero-inflation coefficient (−.363**) is not 'rural schools are advantaged'; it is a comparison of a rural school to a hypothetical suburban school of the same enrollment, a region of the covariate space where few suburban schools exist. No common-support or overlap diagnostic is reported, and no locale × size interaction is estimated even though the entire substantive story is that size operates differently in rural places.
- The by-course severity ranking is a scale artifact and reverses on the absolute scale. On the odds scale (Table 4, Figure 9) the biggest rural/town gaps are Physics C: E&M (rural −43.0%, town −59.5%) and Calculus BC. But on the percentage-point scale from Table 3, the largest rural-suburban gaps are AP Statistics (59.53 − 18.71 = 40.8 pp), Chemistry (37.6 pp), Biology (36.9 pp), and Calculus BC (36.1 pp), while the physics C courses are the SMALLEST (E&M 13.4 pp; Mechanics 20.9 pp). The abstract's claim that gaps are 'smallest for core-adjacent STEM courses and largest for high-math-demand courses' holds only in relative odds; in terms of how many rural schools and students are actually short a course, it is close to backwards.
- The AP Calculus AB 'exception' is entirely a product of the size adjustment and is heavily extrapolated. Unadjusted, rural schools offer Calc AB at 37.92% versus 72.75% suburban (Table 3) — a 34.8 pp deficit. After conditioning on sqrt(enrollment), whose Calc AB coefficient is large (.114***), rural flips to +28.8% higher odds. Given the limited enrollment overlap between rural and suburban schools and the linear-in-sqrt functional form, this is model extrapolation, not a discovered fact about rural schools.
- The AP Physics C: E&M logit shows clear signs of quasi-separation, and it is the column carrying the paper's largest headline gap. The intercept is −25.867 (SE 1.616), roughly triple the next largest (Physics C: Mechanics, −11.990), and the log(proportion Asian) coefficient has SE .097 against .008–.026 in every other column. Plugging plausible covariate values into that model yields a linear predictor near −16 before state effects, which is only reconcilable if the reference-state fixed effect is enormous — the signature of a state with (near) zero offering schools. N is reported as 21,139 in all twelve models, so no separated observations were dropped. The Physics C: Mechanics Asian coefficient (.172, SE .064) shows the same pattern more mildly.
- The 'structural zero' interpretation is a modeling convention presented as a measured construct. Nothing in the data identifies which zeros are structural; the mixture is identified purely by functional form against a count distribution (Figure 1) that is flat rather than Poisson-shaped across 1–12, which means the mixture is doing a great deal of unverifiable work. The paper glosses structural zeros as 'complete absence of an AP program and/or exclusive reliance on DE or IB' (p. 10) — neither of which is in the model. The audit file would readily support a validation the paper does not run: a school with non-STEM AP audits but zero STEM audits is demonstrably not a 'no AP program' zero.
- The outcome is a count out of exactly 12 possible courses, so a zero-inflated binomial is the natural model; Poisson places mass above 12 and cannot respect the ceiling that Figure 1 shows the data reaching. The paper says ZIP 'was supported by AIC and BIC values relative to other count models considered' without naming them (ZINB in particular) or reporting the comparison. Given the flat 1–12 distribution, overdispersion in the positive component is likely.
- Two statistical inconsistencies. First, the paper says 'there is no population about which I am making inferences' and then reports state-clustered SEs and significance stars, and proceeds to interpret results by significance (Model B rural is load-bearing precisely because it is starred at **). It cannot be both. Second, 48 clusters (50 states minus AK/HI in some analyses, or 50–51) with cluster-robust SEs is at the edge where the asymptotics bite and no small-cluster correction is mentioned; 48 locale coefficients across the twelve logits are tested with no multiplicity adjustment.
- Covariate construction is under-documented and partly mismatched to the construct. 'Constants were added prior to log transformation' (p. 6) — the constants are never reported, and for race/ethnicity proportions with many exact zeros (proportion Asian in rural schools) the coefficient on log(p + c) is highly sensitive to c. School SES is proxied by EDGE IPR, a neighborhood measure built from the 25 nearest ACS families, not a school-poverty measure like FRPL; for schools with large attendance areas (disproportionately rural) this is noisier, producing measurement error correlated with the locale variable of interest that can load onto the rural dummy. Only Black, Latinx, and Asian proportions are entered, so the implicit reference is white plus Native American plus other — despite Native American students being flagged in the literature review as the most disadvantaged group.
- The GWLR analysis (Figures 10–11) is the least supported part of the paper and generates some of its most specific claims. Footnote 4 declines to report any estimates 'given the inherent concerns of multicollinearity and sparseness of data at local levels'; footnote 12 drops the state fixed effects that the paper elsewhere treats as necessary; AK and HI are dropped; the adaptive bandwidth value is never given; and there is no uncertainty overlay. Yet the text draws directional conclusions from the maps ('in Iowa most town schools have less availability... in South Carolina the relationship is the opposite'; 'New York state has the largest variation'). Town-versus-suburb local contrasts also require both school types within the bandwidth, which fails across much of the interior West.
- Temporal and denominator construction are thin. Covariates come from a single year (2018–19, per footnote 3, with 11 schools from 2017–18 and 1 from 2016–17) while the outcome is a four-year union, so schools that closed mid-window are effectively defined out of the 'population.' No exposure offset accounts for schools open fewer than four years, which mechanically depresses their 'ever offered' count. The high-school definition — 'schools offering courses for 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th-grade students' — is broad enough to admit K–12 schools, alternative schools, virtual schools, juvenile-justice and special-education placements, and career centers, several of which cannot structurally offer AP and are not evenly distributed across locales. No restriction to NCES regular school type is reported, and N = 21,139 sits above the usual ~20,000 count of regular public high schools.
- Reported Brier scores invite the wrong reading. The lowest Brier in Table 4 is Physics C: E&M (.050), but its base rate is 7.4%, so a null model predicting the base rate scores .069. Converting to skill scores (1 − Brier/null) reverses the ordering: Calc AB .487, Statistics .466, Chemistry .454, Biology .450 versus Physics 2 .234, Physics C: E&M .272, Physics C: Mechanics .328. The models fit worst for exactly the rare courses whose gaps the paper foregrounds — and all Brier scores are in-sample with no cross-validation.
- The unit-of-analysis mismatch in the disproportionality framing (Table 1, Figure 2). The paper motivates the study in terms of students denied opportunities but computes disproportionality over schools, which overweights small rural schools. The student-weighted version is relegated to the supplement and characterized as 'less pronounced' — a concession that the magnitude of the headline gap depends on the choice of unit. Relatedly, Figure 8's '+29.39%' values are percentage-point differences in composition share, while Figure 9's values are genuine percent changes in odds; the same '%' symbol is doing two different jobs in adjacent figures.
- No robustness checks of any kind are reported: no single-year outcome definition, no ZINB, no alternative locale coding, no sensitivity to the log constants, no restriction to schools with any AP program. Most conspicuously, the twelve-category NCES locale codes are described in the Measures section (p. 6) and are in the data, and the Limitations section argues at length that the four-category collapse hides rural heterogeneity — but the finer codes are never used, so the paper's own strongest methodological critique goes untested with data it holds.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Rely on the descriptive layer. Tables 1 and 3 and Figure 8 are population counts, verified to reproduce exactly, and require no modeling assumptions. '48.0% of rural high schools offered no AP STEM course in any of 2015–2019' and 'rural schools are 37.7% of high schools but 20.7% of those offering 4+ AP STEM courses' are as solid as descriptive education statistics get. Cite these directly rather than the model predictions.
- Do not quote 'suburban schools offer nearly three times as many AP STEM courses as rural schools' as an adjusted comparison. The arithmetic behind those combined predictions (5.35 vs 1.81) implies structural-zero probabilities that contradict the Model B coefficients they are said to come from, and enrollment-weighting them reproduces the national raw mean. Treat 5.35 vs 1.81 as approximately the raw locale gap and the ~14% count-model gap (about 0.8 courses) as the size- and SES-adjusted one. If the distinction matters to your argument, ask the author how the combined predictions were evaluated.
- Read the sign flip in Table 2 Model B as the answer to a different question, not as a correction of Model A. Model A ('rural schools have 40.6% higher odds of no structural support') is the policy-relevant descriptive fact. Model B ('rural schools have 30% LOWER odds than an equally sized suburban school') conditions away the very thing that makes rural schools rural. The reported ratio e^-.363 / e^.341 = 0.495 is arithmetically correct but describes a sign reversal, not an attenuation; and in a logit, coefficient changes from adding a strong predictor are partly rescaling (noncollapsibility), so 'school size accounts for much of the relationship' is not licensed without a formal decomposition.
- Do not build on 'rural schools are 28.8% more likely to offer AP Calculus AB.' Unadjusted, they are far less likely (37.9% vs 72.8%). The reversal comes entirely from conditioning on enrollment in a region where rural and suburban schools barely overlap. If you need a claim about Calculus AB, the correct one is that it is the course where the rural deficit is proportionally smallest, not that rural schools have an advantage.
- Reverse the by-course priority ordering if your question is about students. The paper's ranking (physics C and Calculus BC as the worst gaps) is on the odds scale. On the percentage-point scale, AP Statistics (40.8 pp), Chemistry (37.6 pp), and Biology (36.9 pp) are the largest rural-suburban deficits, and the physics C courses are the smallest (13.4 and 20.9 pp). For 'how many rural schools lack the course,' use the Table 3 percentages, not Figure 9.
- Treat the AP Physics C: E&M column of Table 4 as unstable. The intercept of −25.867 and an Asian coefficient SE roughly ten times its neighbors indicate quasi-separation on the state fixed effects. Its locale coefficients (rural −.562, town −.905) may still be directionally right, but they should not be quoted as precise magnitudes, and the claim that this course has the single largest locale gap rests on the paper's least reliable estimates.
- Treat Figures 10 and 11 as exploratory illustration only. No coefficients, standard errors, or bandwidth are reported (footnote 4), the state fixed effects are dropped (footnote 12), and the maps carry no uncertainty. The state-specific readings in the text (Iowa, South Carolina, New York) should not be cited as findings, and the town-versus-suburb local contrast is extrapolated wherever suburban schools are absent from the bandwidth.
- Remember the outcome is audit authorization, not a course taught. A school appears as 'offering' a course if it obtained the AP designation in any one of four years, even if the class never ran or ran once with three students. The paper acknowledges that this overstates availability. If larger, better-staffed schools are more likely to bank authorizations they do not use, or rural schools less likely to complete the audit for a small class, both push the observed gap wider than the true teaching gap. Zeros are more trustworthy than positives here: a four-year zero is strong evidence of genuine unavailability.
- If you are extending this work, verify the school universe before comparing to other AP counts. N = 21,139 with a definition of 'any school serving grades 9–12' likely includes K–12, alternative, virtual, and special-purpose schools that cannot structurally offer AP; the paper does not report restricting to NCES regular high schools. The locale-share denominators in Table 1 and Figure 2 depend on this choice.
- Prefer the supplementary student-weighted disproportionality figure when the argument is about students rather than institutions. The paper reports that those relationships are 'less pronounced,' so the school-weighted headline is the larger of the two available numbers.
- Ignore the significance stars when weighing magnitudes. With the full population and N = 21,139, effectively any non-trivial coefficient will star, 48 locale tests are run across Table 4 with no multiplicity adjustment, and the author's own statement that inference is not meaningful here is the right one. Judge the coefficients by size, not by p-values.
- Before quantitatively reusing any covariate coefficient, note that the constants added inside the log transformations are never reported. The log(proportion Black/Latinx/Asian) and log(IPR) coefficients are not reproducible or comparable across studies without that value.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This paper's evidentiary structure has two clearly separable layers, and readers should treat them very differently.

The descriptive layer is about as strong as descriptive education research gets, and it is where the paper's durable contribution lies. The unit of observation is the complete population of AP audit records for 2015–2019 joined to CCD/EDGE, with non-offering schools explicitly added back (p. 5) — so there is no AP-offering selection problem, and no sampling uncertainty. I recomputed essentially every reported descriptive figure and they all reproduce: Table 1's rural 1+ rate (3,826/7,967 = 48.02%), Table 3's national rates (Calculus AB 11,094/21,139 = 52.48%; Physics C: E&M 1,569/21,139 = 7.42%), and every Figure 8 disproportionality value to two decimals (suburban Physics C: E&M 846/1,569 = 53.92% minus a 24.53% population share = +29.39%; rural Calculus BC 885/5,223 = 16.94%, giving 37.69 − 16.94 = 20.75%). That level of arithmetic cleanliness is uncommon and should raise a reader's confidence in the tables substantially. The core factual claim — that in 2015–2019 nearly half of rural U.S. public high schools obtained no AP STEM authorization at all, versus roughly one in five suburban schools, and that rural underrepresentation widens monotonically as the course-count threshold rises — needs no modeling and should be treated as established.

The regression layer is competently executed but supports weaker and narrower claims than the prose around it. Three problems in particular change how specific numbers should be read.

First, the paper's most-quotable number is probably not the estimand it is labeled as. On p. 11 the count-only predictions are computed explicitly 'using the suburban means of the covariates' and are internally consistent (5.869 × e^-.152 = 5.041, matching the reported 5.039 for rural). The combined predictions immediately following — suburb 5.35, city 3.64, town 2.41, rural 1.81, yielding 'nearly three times as many as rural schools' — are described as being 'with school sociodemographic and enrollment controls,' but they cannot be evaluated at common covariate values. Backing out the implied structural-zero probabilities from combined = (1 − pi) × lambda gives pi = .088 suburban, .358 city, .512 town, .641 rural. Model B's zero-inflation component says the opposite: rural OR = e^-.363 = 0.696, i.e. rural schools have LOWER conditional odds of a structural zero than an equally sized suburban school. Enrollment-weighting the four combined predictions across the Table 1 locale counts returns 3.20 courses nationally, which is consistent with these being each locale's own marginal mean. So the paper presents a genuinely adjusted gap of about 14% (roughly 0.8 courses) and an essentially unadjusted gap of about 3x within two paragraphs, both under the same 'with controls' label. The 3x figure is the one that will be cited; readers should cite it as descriptive.

Second, the school-size adjustment that structures the whole Table 2 discussion is a mediator adjustment presented as a confounder adjustment. The paper's own literature review (p. 4, and again in the Discussion) argues that small size is constitutive of rurality and that rural size limits specialty staffing. Conditioning on sqrt(enrollment) therefore asks 'among schools of equal size, is rural worse?' — a controlled direct effect requiring no unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding, which district wealth, STEM teacher supply, and geographic isolation all violate. The paper reports the shift as an odds ratio that 'nearly halves,' e^-.363 / e^.341 = 0.4946. The arithmetic is right, but the underlying quantity moved from OR 1.41 to OR 0.70 — a sign reversal, not an attenuation — and the plain-English implication of Model B (rural schools of a given size are LESS likely to be structural zeros than suburban schools) is never stated. Adding to this, in logistic and log-link models coefficients change when a strong covariate is added even absent any confounding (noncollapsibility), so 'school size importantly accounts for much of the relationship' (p. 11) is not licensed by a raw coefficient comparison across two models whose intercepts also move from 1.981 to 5.351. A KHB-style decomposition or a locale × size interaction would have settled this; neither is present.

Third, the by-course results are reported on a scale that inverts their policy meaning. Table 4 and Figure 9 rank gaps by odds, where the worst are Physics C: E&M (rural −43.0%, town −59.5%) and Calculus BC (rural −38.7%, town −43.2%). But odds-scale gaps are mechanically large for rare outcomes. Computing rural-suburban percentage-point differences from Table 3 gives a nearly reversed ordering: Statistics 40.8 pp, Chemistry 37.6 pp, Biology 36.9 pp, Calculus BC 36.1 pp, Calculus AB 34.8 pp — versus Physics C: E&M 13.4 pp, Physics 2 16.3 pp, Physics C: Mechanics 20.9 pp. The abstract's summary that 'rural/town availability gaps are smallest for core-adjacent STEM courses and largest for high-math-demand courses' is true in relative odds and roughly false in absolute terms. The Discussion half-notices this ('much of this ranking is disproportionately driven by their limited offerings in rural and town schools') but does not follow the thought to its conclusion. The same tension explains the Calculus AB 'exception': rural schools offer it at 37.92% versus 72.75% suburban, yet the adjusted odds are 28.8% higher for rural — a reversal produced entirely by conditioning on sqrt(enrollment) (coefficient .114***) in a region where the rural and suburban enrollment distributions barely overlap. No overlap or common-support diagnostic is reported anywhere, and given the linear-in-sqrt specification this is extrapolation.

On estimation execution, several smaller items compound. The outcome is a count out of exactly twelve possible courses; a zero-inflated binomial is the natural family, and Figure 1 shows the data reaching the ceiling. ZIP puts mass above 12 and, more importantly, the positive part of Figure 1 is close to flat from 1 to about 8 rather than humped around the fitted mean of ~5.9 — a shape that a Poisson count component fits poorly and that suggests overdispersion. The paper says ZIP was 'supported by AIC and BIC values relative to other count models considered' without naming them; whether ZINB was among them matters and is not knowable from the text. The 'structural zero' label is also a modeling convention, not a measurement: nothing in the data identifies which zeros are structural, the mixture is identified purely by functional form, and the paper's substantive gloss (no AP program at all, or exclusive reliance on DE/IB) is not in the model. The audit file supports an easy validation the paper skips — a school with non-STEM AP audits and zero STEM audits is demonstrably not an 'absence of an AP program' zero.

The Physics C: E&M logit deserves specific caution because it carries the paper's largest headline gap. Its intercept is −25.867 (SE 1.616) against −11.990 for Physics C: Mechanics and −9.830 for Computer Science A, and its log(proportion Asian) coefficient is .175 with SE .097 — roughly ten times the SE in the other columns (.008 to .026). Plugging plausible covariate values into that model yields a linear predictor near −16 before state effects, reconcilable only if some state fixed effect is enormous, which is the signature of quasi-separation. All twelve models report N = 21,139, so no separated observations were dropped; states with no offering schools would have diverging coefficients rather than being removed. Physics C: Mechanics shows a milder version (Asian .172, SE .064). Note also that Physics C: E&M is the one course where the raw rural rate (2.87%) exceeds the raw town rate (2.29%), yet the fitted town coefficient (−.905) is far more negative than rural (−.562) — the size adjustment could produce that, but combined with the separation signals it argues for treating that column's magnitudes as unstable.

The Brier scores in Table 4 are correctly reported but easy to misread. Physics C: E&M has the lowest Brier (.050), which looks like the best-fitting model; against a null model predicting its 7.4% base rate, whose Brier is .069, the skill score is only .272. Converting all twelve gives Calculus AB .487, Statistics .466, Chemistry .454, Biology .450 at the top and Physics 2 .234, Computer Science Principles .224, Physics C: E&M .272 at the bottom. The models discriminate worst precisely for the rare courses whose gaps the paper foregrounds, and none of the scores are cross-validated.

The GWLR section is the weakest link between analysis and claim. Footnote 4 declines to report estimates because of multicollinearity and local sparseness; footnote 12 removes the state fixed effects the paper treats as essential elsewhere and drops Alaska and Hawaii; the adaptive bandwidth is never reported; and no uncertainty is displayed. Yet the text draws directional, state-specific conclusions from Figures 10 and 11 — Iowa's town schools disadvantaged, South Carolina's advantaged, New York most variable. GWLR local coefficients are known to produce apparent spatial structure from noise, and a town-versus-suburb contrast is only estimable where both locale types are inside the bandwidth, which fails across much of the interior West. These are the paper's least supported claims and should be read as hypothesis-generating.

Finally, some construction details limit reuse. Covariates come from a single year (2018–19, footnote 3) while the outcome is a four-year union with no exposure offset for schools open fewer than four years, and schools closing mid-window are effectively excluded from the 'population.' The four-year union means no student's actual experience corresponds to the count for schools with rotating offerings, though for the zero side it is a genuinely strong statement (a four-year audit zero is real unavailability). School SES is EDGE IPR — a neighborhood measure from the 25 nearest ACS families, not school poverty — which for large rural attendance areas introduces measurement error correlated with the locale variable of interest, potentially loading onto the rural dummy. Only Black, Latinx, and Asian proportions enter, leaving Native American students in the implicit reference despite the literature review flagging them as most disadvantaged. The constants added inside the log transforms are never reported, which makes the log-proportion coefficients neither reproducible nor comparable. The 'high school' definition (any school serving grades 9–12) is broad enough to admit K–12, alternative, virtual, and career schools with no restriction to NCES regular type; N = 21,139 sits above the usual regular-high-school count, and the locale denominators in Table 1 and Figure 2 depend on this. And there are no robustness checks at all — most notably, the twelve-category NCES locale codes are described in Measures and are in the data, and the Limitations section argues forcefully that the four-category collapse hides rural heterogeneity, yet the finer codes are never used to test the paper's own best methodological insight.

Net assessment: adequate. The paper delivers a genuinely valuable, verifiable descriptive portrait of a population that had not been mapped at this resolution, and its non-causal framing is appropriate throughout. The regression apparatus is competently built but is asked to carry claims — a 3x adjusted locale gap, a rural Calculus AB advantage, a physics-first ranking of gap severity, state-specific spatial conclusions — that the reported estimates do not straightforwardly support.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (low confidence)

The literature review is well-organized, honest about measurement limits, and unusually current in two corners (computer science education and the rural-measurement critique), and it genuinely engages the school-size-versus-rurality confound rather than dodging it. But it rests heavily on advocacy and think-tank reports without flagging their provenance, leaves an unreconciled conflict between its own headline descriptives and the prior national estimate it claims to extend (88% vs. 66.7% of city schools offering an AP STEM course), and omits the sociological frame (Lucas's effectively maintained inequality), the CRDC-based AP-access literature, and the canonical AP review that would let readers place its contribution accurately. The novelty claim is defensible but only because of stacked qualifiers readers should notice.

**Strengths:**

- The size-versus-locale confound is named in the review (p. 5: rural schools 'are often characterized by small school size, both of which... are associated with limited advanced course offerings') and then tested directly rather than assumed away, via the Model A / Model B contrast in Table 2. Many papers in this space cite Monk & Haller (1993) and then ignore what it implies; this one builds its central analysis around it.
- The audit-versus-enrollment distinction is handled with real care (Limitations, p. 20; footnote 2). The paper states plainly that audit data overestimate availability while enrollment data confound availability with student dispositions and enrollment barriers, and it maps each to the corresponding tier of its OTL framework. Readers can trust the paper's account of what its measure does and does not capture.
- Computer science education coverage is current and peer-reviewed (Childs et al. 2024 in Review of Research in Education; Warner et al. 2019, 2021; Fletcher & Warner 2021; Garvin et al. 2024; Code.org 2024; Hodges 2025), and it is integrated rather than decorative — the CS findings on pp. 15-19 are read back against the broadening-participation-in-computing agenda.
- The rural-measurement critique (pp. 20-21) is the strongest scholarly passage in the paper. DeYoung (1987), Theodori (2003), Cromartie & Bucholtz (2008), and Drescher et al. (2022) are used to make a substantive argument about NCES locale codes rather than as a limitations-section throat-clearing, and the argument is earned by the paper's own regional results.
- The paper correctly reports the internal complication in Theokas & Saaris (2013) on p. 4 — that SES gaps in AP *program presence* are small (91% vs. 93%) while gaps in AP *breadth* are large. This is the right reading of that report and is the exact distinction the paper's own design exploits.

**Weaknesses:**

- The paper cites S. Mann et al. (2017) on p. 5 for the figure that 88% of city schools offered at least one AP STEM course in 2015, and then reports in Table 1 (p. 7) that 66.71% of city schools offered 1+ AP STEM course over 2015-2019. The gap runs the wrong way — Boles's four-year union measure should be *more* generous than a single-year figure — which points to a sample or denominator difference (most likely inclusion of alternative, special-purpose, and very small schools in the 21,139). The paper never reconciles the two numbers, even though S. Mann et al. is the study it says it 'expands upon' (p. 19). Readers comparing across studies will be misled if they take the two sets of percentages as commensurable.
- The novelty claim on p. 2 — 'for the first time, using school-level regression analyses to isolate and estimate geographic variation in the availability and spatial distribution of AP STEM course offerings' — survives only through accumulated qualifiers (school-level AND geographic AND STEM AND per-course). School-level regression on AP offerings is not new (Iatarola, Conger & Long 2011; Barnard-Brak et al. 2011; and, I believe, Klugman's work on the AP 'arms race' in California high schools and Klopfenstein 2004 on Texas AP offerings, neither of which is cited). What is genuinely new is national population coverage of the audit file, per-course STEM disaggregation, and the geographically weighted models.
- The Civil Rights Data Collection is never mentioned. CRDC is the standard federal census of AP course offerings by school and is the basis for much of the AP-availability equity literature; a reader cannot tell from this paper how audit-based availability compares to CRDC-based availability, or whether the national school-level patterns reported here replicate what CRDC-based work already shows. This is the most consequential omission for evaluating the data contribution.
- Xu, Solanki & Fink (2021, AERJ) is cited twice (pp. 2, 20) only for the proposition that AP is the largest acceleration pathway — never for its access findings. If my recollection is right that they used national school-level CRDC data and explicitly separated whether a school offers AP from whether students participate, it is the closest published antecedent to this paper's question and the one most in need of engagement. (Flagging with moderate confidence; readers should check the paper themselves.)
- The discussion's dismissal of online delivery (p. 19) — 'we saw that current online learning models were differentially successful, particularly underserving students from rural areas' — is sourced entirely to COVID emergency-remote-instruction evidence (Dorn et al. 2020 McKinsey, Lewis et al. 2021 NWEA, Pier et al. 2021, B. Mann et al. 2021, Coleman et al. 2021). Emergency remote schooling in spring 2020 is weak evidence about deliberately designed online AP delivery in small rural schools, and Dorn et al. is a consulting-firm projection rather than measurement. The better-suited studies are cited in the paper — Hart et al. (2023) on online course-taking expanding curricular options, Mader et al. (2025) on Tennessee's AP Access for All — but only in the future-work list (pp. 20-21), not where the claim is made.
- Several load-bearing empirical claims rest on advocacy, vendor, or consulting reports presented without provenance caveats: Chatterji et al. (2021, Center for American Progress) for school size, Native American access, and city rankings; Theokas & Saaris (2013, Education Trust); S. Mann et al. (2017, Education Commission of the States with the College Board — i.e., co-produced by the AP program's owner); Handwerk et al. (2008, ETS); Gagnon & Mattingly (2015, Carsey brief); Malkus (2016, AEI). Some of this is unavoidable in a niche where descriptive national AP facts live in gray literature, but the paper treats these interchangeably with peer-reviewed findings.
- Lucas's (2001) effectively maintained inequality is absent, and it is the theory that best fits the paper's own central pattern: near-universal AP program presence with large disparities in breadth and in the most advanced courses. The OTL triad from Greeno & Gresalfi (2008) scopes the study but explains none of the results.
- For a paper whose contribution is partly spatial, there is essentially no spatial-analysis or spatial-inequality literature — geographically weighted logistic regression is introduced with a citation to the R package (Bivand & Yu 2023) and nothing else. Tate's 'geography of opportunity' framing in Educational Researcher (2008, as I recall it) and the broader GWR methodological literature are both missing.
- The intro (p. 2) cites Theokas & Saaris (2013) alongside Oakes (1990) to support the claim that low-SES students are less likely to have advanced STEM coursework available — which is in tension with the paper's own more careful reading of the same report on p. 4, where it reports that SES differences in AP program availability were minimal. The source is used loosely in one place and precisely in another.
- Long, Conger & McGhee (2019, Educational Researcher) asks whether less-resourced schools can successfully implement AP science courses. Its cautionary implication is never carried into the conclusion (p. 21), which recommends expansion without qualification. The paper cites the evidence that complicates its policy recommendation and then does not use it.
- The claim that rural teachers are less likely to hold STEM degrees (p. 19) rests on Carlsen & Monk (1992) and Barton (2012) — a thirty-year-old study and a practitioner brief — for a claim about the contemporary rural STEM workforce.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before citing this paper's descriptive percentages next to figures from S. Mann et al. (2017), NCES (2009), or Malkus (2016), check the sample definitions. This paper's denominator is all 21,139 public schools serving grades 9-12, which almost certainly includes alternative, virtual, special-purpose, and very small schools that other AP-availability estimates exclude. The 66.71% city figure in Table 1 and the 88% city figure quoted on p. 5 are not measuring the same population.
- Cite this paper for what is actually distinctive: the first national, population-level, per-course adjusted estimates of AP STEM *offering* by NCES locale, plus the geographically weighted maps showing that town-suburb gaps vary within states (Figures 10-11). Cite Iatarola, Conger & Long (2011) for the determinants of school-level advanced course offerings, Monk & Haller (1993) for size as the dominant structural predictor, and Gagnon & Mattingly (2015, 2016) for rurality gradients in AP access — this paper extends those rather than displacing them.
- Read alongside a CRDC-based account of AP availability, which this paper does not engage at all. Xu, Solanki & Fink (2021, AERJ), which the paper cites for a different purpose, is the natural companion if (as I believe) it separates school-level AP availability from student participation using national data.
- For the field's synthesis of what is known about AP access and effectiveness, look for Kolluri's Review of Educational Research treatment of AP (2018, as I recall it) — an omission that matters because it is where a reader would find the contested evidence on whether AP expansion delivers the benefits the paper's conclusion assumes. I am reasonably but not fully confident of this citation; verify it rather than repeating it on my say-so.
- For school-level regression antecedents on AP offerings that this paper does not cite, look for Klugman's work on AP course offerings and school composition in California high schools, and Klopfenstein (2004, Economics of Education Review) on AP offerings and minority composition in Texas. I am moderately confident both exist in roughly this form; treat them as leads to verify, not as established citations.
- Treat the paper's causal language about school size with care. The paper shows that adding enrollment flips the sign of all three locale coefficients in the zero-inflation model (Table 2, p. 10) and reads this as size 'accounting for' the locale relationship. Rurality plausibly causes small schools, which makes enrollment a mediator rather than a confounder; the estimates in Model B are therefore 'the locale gap not operating through size,' not 'the true locale gap.' The consolidation and small-schools literature (Howley and colleagues, on size and the size-by-poverty interaction — cited from memory, worth verifying) frames this problem and is absent here.
- Read the results through effectively maintained inequality (Lucas 2001, American Journal of Sociology) rather than through the OTL triad. The paper's signature findings — near-parity in AP Calculus AB and AP Biology, enormous rural and town deficits in AP Physics C and Calculus BC — are the textbook EMI pattern of inequality migrating from access-to-a-level toward qualitative differentiation within it. The paper's own OTL framing does not generate this prediction.
- Do not take the discussion's dismissal of online delivery (p. 19) as an evidence-based conclusion. It is grounded in COVID emergency-remote-instruction studies, not in studies of designed online advanced coursework. For the relevant evidence, go to Hart, Linden, Jacob & Loeb (2023) on online course-taking and curricular expansion and Mader et al. (2025) on Tennessee's AP Access for All — both cited in this paper but only as future work — and to the IES evaluation of online Algebra I for expanding access in small and rural schools (Heppen and colleagues; cited from memory, verify before use).
- Verify the STEM teacher-supply statistic before repeating it. The claim that newly certified STEM teachers declined by over a third within a decade (p. 3) rests entirely on Nguyen (2025); the related claim about rural teachers' STEM credentials (p. 19) rests on Carlsen & Monk (1992) and a 2012 practitioner brief.
- Note the interdisciplinary asymmetry when placing this paper. Its computer science education and rural-measurement literatures are current and peer-reviewed; its economics-of-education engagement is thin (Callen & Stoddard 2024 and Conger et al. 2009 essentially alone, with no engagement of the contested returns-to-AP evidence — e.g., Jackson's work on the Texas AP Incentive Program, cited from memory); its sociology of education stops at Oakes and Kelly; and its spatial-analysis literature is effectively an R package citation. Readers coming from economics or from geography should expect to supply that context themselves.
- When repeating the paper's summaries of prior studies, note their scope conditions, which the paper generally does not: Conger, Long & Iatarola (2009) is Florida administrative data (and its central point is that most advanced course-taking disparity is within-school rather than in access to AP-offering schools); Zarate & Pachon (2006) is California; Iatarola et al. (2011) is, as I recall, Florida and New York City. None of these is national, though the paper's prose presents them in an undifferentiated list of findings.
- Read the OTL framing (pp. 2-3) as scoping rather than as analysis. It justifies studying availability alone and supplies the vocabulary for the audit-versus-enrollment limitation, but no coefficient, specification, or interpretation depends on Greeno and Gresalfi. Note also the unaddressed tension with the OTL tradition's own standards: SIMS/TIMSS-era OTL is about enacted content coverage, and AP audit approval for a course title is a distal proxy for it.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Overall placement.** This is a competent, readable literature review that does the basic job well — it establishes that AP is the dominant advanced-coursework pathway, that availability varies by race, SES, size, and locale, and that the existing evidence on locale is mostly descriptive or district-level. Its structure is logical: OTL framing, then domain (advanced STEM), then vehicle (AP), then the axes of inequity (organizational constraints, race/ethnicity, SES, locale), converging on a research question. Where it falls short is not in coverage of the obvious, but in three specific places: it does not reconcile its own numbers with the literature it says it extends; it omits the federal data source and the review article that would let readers calibrate its contribution; and it does not engage the sociological theory that fits its findings better than the theory it adopts.

**The novelty claim (p. 2).** The claim is that this is the first study 'using school-level regression analyses to isolate and estimate geographic variation in the availability and spatial distribution of AP STEM course offerings, both in aggregate as a domain and disaggregated by individual courses.' Read carefully, this is four conjoined qualifiers, and each one is doing work. School-level regression on advanced course offerings is Iatarola, Conger & Long (2011), which the paper cites and correctly credits (p. 2, p. 4). Locale gradients in AP are Gagnon & Mattingly (2015, 2016), also cited. STEM-specific descriptive locale patterns are S. Mann et al. (2017), also cited. What is left after the qualifiers — national school-level adjusted estimates, disaggregated to individual AP STEM courses, with geographically weighted spatial variation — is a real contribution, and the paper's own two-limitation setup on p. 2 (Gagnon & Mattingly is district-level; Gagnon & Mattingly is not STEM-specific) is a fair statement of the gap. My caution to readers is narrower: the phrase 'for the first time' is doing rhetorical work that the substantive claim does not need, and readers should attribute the size-and-composition determinants of AP offerings to Iatarola et al. and the rural-AP gradient to Gagnon & Mattingly, not to this paper. I would add that if Klugman's California AP-offerings work and Klopfenstein's (2004) Texas AP work exist as I remember them, they are school-level regressions on AP offerings that predate this paper by a decade or more and are uncited — which does not defeat the qualified claim but does mean the paper undersells how much school-level regression work on AP supply already exists.

**The unreconciled descriptive conflict.** This is my most concrete finding. On p. 5 the paper writes: 'In 2015, 92% of city schools offered at least one AP course, and 88% offered at least one STEM AP course (S. Mann et al., 2017).' In Table 1 (p. 7) the paper's own data give 3,409 of 5,110 city schools, or 66.71%, offering 1+ AP STEM course — and that figure uses a four-year union rule (a school counts if it completed the audit in any of 2015-16 through 2018-19, described on p. 6), which should make it *more* generous than a single-year measure, not less. A 21-point gap in the wrong direction is a sample-composition signal: this paper's population includes every school serving any of grades 9-12 in CCD, which will sweep in alternative schools, virtual schools, special-education and juvenile-justice schools, and very small programs that prior AP-availability estimates typically exclude. That may well be a defensible design choice — the paper's argument is precisely about the schools other analyses drop — but the review never surfaces the choice as a point of contrast with the literature, and the discussion (p. 19) says this study 'expands upon findings from S. Mann et al. (2017)' as if the two sets of numbers sat on the same scale. Readers should not quote this paper's percentages alongside Mann's, Malkus's 'seven in 10 US high schools offer at least one AP course' (p. 3), or NCES (2009) figures without checking denominators first.

**Accuracy of characterizations.** On the whole the paper's summaries of prior work are accurate in direction, and one is notably careful: the treatment of Theokas & Saaris (2013) on p. 4 correctly reports the report's internally complicating result — near-parity in AP *program* presence by SES (91% vs. 93%) but a near-doubling of the odds of attending a school without a full AP core — and this distinction is exactly the one the paper's own design exploits. Two cautions. First, the same source is used more loosely in the introduction (p. 2), where it is paired with Oakes (1990) to support the flat claim that low-SES students are less likely to have advanced STEM coursework available; the p. 4 reading is the right one and the p. 2 reading overreaches. Second, the paper presents Conger, Long & Iatarola (2009), Theokas & Saaris (2013), Handwerk et al. (2008), and Chatterji et al. (2021) as a single undifferentiated evidence stream on race and AP availability, when these are, respectively, a Florida administrative-data study, a national Education Trust report, an ETS report, and a Center for American Progress report. Conger et al.'s substantive contribution — that most of the racial gap in advanced course-taking is within-school rather than in access to AP-offering schools — is a finding in real tension with this paper's framing of availability as the binding constraint, and it goes unremarked. The Monk & Haller (1993) and Iatarola et al. (2011) characterizations are, to my knowledge, accurate: size drives breadth of offerings, small schools must privilege graduation-required core courses, and a critical mass of high-achieving entering students is the strongest single predictor of AP offerings.

**Size versus locale.** This is the dimension where the paper's literature engagement is strongest analytically and weakest interpretively. It is strong because the review explicitly names the confound (p. 5: rural schools are characterized by small size, and both are associated with limited offerings) and then builds the empirical design around it, reporting Models A and B with and without enrollment (Table 2, p. 10) and being candid that the locale coefficients flip sign when size enters. It is weak because the paper does not follow the interpretive question that Monk & Haller (1993) and the small-schools literature pose: if rurality causes small schools, enrollment is a mediator, and 'controlling for' it removes the very mechanism through which locale operates. The paper's discussion (p. 19) treats the Model B estimates as the more credible ones ('school size importantly accounts for much of the relationship') without saying that the Model A estimates are the ones a reader interested in the total effect of locale should want. The consolidation and school-size literature — Howley and colleagues on size, poverty, and the size-by-SES interaction, cited here from memory — is the natural place this question has been worked out, and it is absent from the review.

**Audit versus enrollment.** The paper's handling here is genuinely good and readers can rely on it. Footnote 2 correctly notes that a student can sit an AP exam without her school holding the audit, and that the school of record must complete the audit for the AP designation to appear on a transcript — including for courses taken online. The Limitations section (p. 20) states the asymmetry cleanly: audit data overestimate availability; enrollment data confound availability with dispositions and with explicit and implicit enrollment barriers. What the review does not supply is any prior literature on the validity of AP-offering measures — how often audit-approved courses are actually run in a given year, or how audit-based counts compare to CRDC or to school-reported course catalogs. Since the whole contribution rests on the audit file being a better availability measure than the alternatives, the absence of any validation literature (or of CRDC as a comparison point) leaves a load-bearing claim unsupported by anything but reasoning.

**The OTL frame.** Greeno & Gresalfi's (2008) availability / accessibility / disposition triad, traced back through McDonnell (1995) and Floden (2002) to SIMS and TIMSS, occupies about a page and a half (pp. 2-3) and returns twice: to justify studying availability alone while pointing to the companion paper on accessibility (Boles & Domingue, 2023), and to name what audit and enrollment data respectively confound (p. 20). That is more than decorative — it is doing scoping and interpretive work — but it is not load-bearing: no hypothesis, no covariate, and no coefficient interpretation depends on it, and the paper's substantive findings would survive its removal intact. There is also an unacknowledged tension. The OTL tradition the paper invokes is specifically about *enacted content coverage* — the SIMS and TIMSS instruments distinguished content made available in the classroom from content students could answer correctly, as the paper itself says on p. 2 — and 'the school holds AP audit approval for this course title' is about as distal a proxy for content coverage as one could construct. The Porter and Schmidt strand of OTL measurement work, which is where that problem is confronted, is not engaged. Separately, Carroll (1963) is cited in support of 'dispositions'; Carroll's model is about time, perseverance, and aptitude, which maps onto disposition only loosely.

**Discussion sourcing.** The online-learning passage on p. 19 is the weakest sourcing in the paper. Its claim is normative and strong — that moving programming online is 'short-sighted,' a lesson the field supposedly learned during COVID — and the support is five COVID emergency-remote-instruction sources, one of which (Dorn et al. 2020) is a McKinsey scenario projection rather than a measurement study. Emergency remote instruction during a pandemic is close to the least informative possible evidence about deliberately designed online AP delivery, and the paper's own citation list contains the better evidence: Hart, Linden, Jacob & Loeb (2023) on online course-taking expanding curricular options, and Mader et al. (2025) on Tennessee's AP Access for All. Both appear only in the future-directions list (pp. 20-21), where they are recommended as studies that should be done rather than used as evidence that already bears on the claim made two pages earlier. The rural teacher-supply passage is better sourced but leans on Showalter et al. (2019), Peterson et al. (2015), Taie & Lewis (2022), and Monk (2007) — a mix of advocacy report, regional study, and federal survey first-look — with the specific claim about rural teachers' STEM credentials resting on Carlsen & Monk (1992) and Barton (2012).

**Interdisciplinary placement.** The paper sits most comfortably in rural education and CS education, less comfortably in economics of education, sociology of education, and geography. In economics, Callen & Stoddard (2024) and Conger et al. (2009) are essentially the whole engagement; the contested literature on whether AP expansion delivers benefits — which is directly relevant to a paper whose conclusion (p. 21) is 'direct resources to expand advanced STEM coursework... into more rural and town-located schools' — is represented only by Long, Conger & McGhee (2019), whose cautionary finding about implementation in less-resourced communities is cited on p. 3 and then not carried into the conclusion. In sociology, Oakes (1990, 2005) and Kelly (2009) anchor the tracking discussion, but Lucas's effectively maintained inequality is missing, and it is the frame that would have explained the paper's central empirical result: gaps in AP *program presence* are modest and partly reverse under controls, while gaps in *breadth* and in the most advanced courses (AP Physics C: E&M, rural -23.09%; AP Calculus BC, rural -20.75%, p. 14) are enormous. That is EMI almost by definition, and reading the paper through it makes the findings more interesting, not less. In geography, the paper runs geographically weighted logistic regression across twelve outcomes and cites, for the entire spatial apparatus, one R package. Neither the GWR methodological literature nor the education-specific geography-of-opportunity strand appears, which is a striking gap for a paper whose author describes her research as examining how space supports and constrains learning opportunities.

**Limits of my assessment.** I have not verified any of the cited reports against their originals, and several of the most consequential ones — S. Mann et al. (2017), Gagnon & Mattingly (2015, 2016), Theokas & Saaris (2013), Chatterji et al. (2021), Handwerk et al. (2008) — are gray literature I know only at second hand. My claims about what Iatarola et al. (2011) and Conger et al. (2009) found, and about the scope of Xu, Solanki & Fink (2021), are from memory and should be checked. Every uncited work I have named is offered as a lead to verify, not as an established citation; I am confident about Lucas (2001) and Monk & Haller (1993), reasonably confident about Kolluri's RER review, Klopfenstein (2004), and Tate (2008), and less confident about the specific Klugman, Howley, Heppen, and Jackson references, which I have flagged as such in the suggestions rather than asserted. Readers should treat the internal inconsistencies I identify — the 88% versus 66.71% conflict, the Theokas & Saaris usage across pp. 2 and 4, and the online-learning citation misallocation between pp. 19 and 21 — as the findings here with the firmest footing, since those rest entirely on the paper's own text.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The prose is clear, the section headings are declarative findings that make the paper unusually navigable, and — remarkably for a paper this number-dense — nearly every figure quoted in the text reproduces exactly from Tables 1, 3 and 4 when recomputed. The problems are not arithmetic but framing and labeling: the abstract overstates the course-level result and omits the school-size finding the paper itself calls critical; two of the four bar-chart exhibits (Figures 2 and 8) carry an x-axis label that describes a quantity they do not plot, and Figure 2's note describes a third quantity again; and the paper's most-quotable headline number (suburban schools offer 'nearly three times as many' courses as rural) cannot be reconciled with the adjusted model it is presented as coming from.

**Strengths:**

- Text–table numeric fidelity is excellent. Every percentage, odds ratio, and disproportionality figure I recomputed from Tables 1, 3, and 4 matched to rounding: 62.24% offering 1+ (13,157/21,139), 7,982 zeros (37.76%), suburb 24.53%/41.43% and rural 37.69%/20.70% of the 4+ group, exp(.375)=45.50%, exp(.341)=40.64%, exp(.019)=1.92%, Calc AB 52.48%, Biology 44.64%, Chemistry 36.84%, Physics 2 10.17%, Physics C Mech 12.80%, Physics C E&M 7.42%, and all ten disproportionality figures on p.13 (suburb +29.39/+26.58/+24.72/+23.66/+22.39; rural −23.09/−22.34/−20.74/−20.73/−20.71). Footnote 11's 13.61% town share is right too. A reader can quote descriptive numbers from this prose with confidence.
- Declarative section headings ('Joint Consideration of Locale and School Size Is Critical to Understand AP STEM Availability') let a reader skim the results and reconstruct the argument from the headings alone. This is the paper's best structural decision.
- The structural-vs-sampling-zero distinction is explained plainly on pp.9–10 before the ZIP results appear, so a reader unfamiliar with zero-inflated models can follow the two-component logic.
- Figures 5 and 9 plot 95% confidence intervals, which makes visible several nulls the prose narrates without qualification — the figures are, on this point, more honest than the text.
- The discussion is candid about a real artifact: 'With the exception of AP Calculus BC, these are also the least-offered courses nationwide, meaning that much of this ranking is disproportionately driven by their limited offerings in rural and town schools' (p.20). This is exactly the caveat a skeptical reader would raise, and the author raises it first.
- The limitations section is unusually substantive on measurement — the audit-vs-enrollment distinction and the critique of NCES locale codes are both framed in ways that constrain rather than inflate the claims.
- Table 4's ranking claims check out.
