The town gaps are, in order, Physics C E&M (−.905), Calc BC (−.566), Physics 2 (−.466), Physics C Mech (−.461), CS A (−.448) — so 'the largest locale-based availability gaps are town-suburban gaps in AP Physics C: E&M and AP Calculus BC' (p.15) is correct, as is the discussion's top-five list.

**Weaknesses:**

- Abstract overstates the course-level finding. It says rural and town schools offer fewer courses 'both in terms of the total number of courses available and the likelihood of offering each course.' The body directly contradicts this: after controls, rural schools have 28.8% and town schools 17.8% HIGHER odds of offering AP Calculus AB (Table 4, +.253 and +.164). The conclusion's item (3) states this correctly ('outside of the three most popular, core-adjacent courses'); the abstract does not.
- Abstract omits school size entirely, even though the paper's own results heading calls the joint consideration of locale and school size 'critical,' the discussion calls school size 'a critical predictor,' and conclusion item (2) lists it as a headline finding. A reader who stops at the abstract takes away a pure locale story and misses that adding enrollment flips the sign of all three zero-inflation locale coefficients (Table 2: city .375→−.038, rural .341→−.363, town .019→−.192).
- The 'high-math-demand' category, which the abstract uses to characterize where gaps are largest, is never enumerated and does not survive the paper's own footnote-10 definition. That footnote includes 'AP courses which are mathematics courses themselves' — which makes Calculus AB (the reversed-gap exception), Calculus BC (the second-largest gap), and Statistics (a middling gap) all high-math-demand. Meanwhile AP Computer Science A, named in the largest-gap list, is neither a math course nor calculus-based. Conclusion item (4) has to bolt on 'with the exception of AP Calculus AB' to keep the claim alive; the abstract does not.
- Figures 2 and 8 are mislabeled. Both x-axes read 'Percent of U.S. Public High Schools,' but the bars plot each locale's SHARE of the course-offering subset. In Figure 2's '1+' pane the city bar sits near 26% — which is 3,409/13,157 = 25.9% (composition), not 3,409/21,139 = 16.1% (percent of all US high schools, what the axis says) and not 66.71% (percent of city schools, what the caption and note imply). Figure 8's CALCAB suburb bar reads ~34% = 3,773/11,094, not 17.9% and not Table 3's 72.75%. Figure 2's note compounds this by describing 'the proportion of schools in each locale offering 1+, 2+, 3+, 4+, and 5+' — which is Table 1's percentage rows, a different quantity from what is drawn. Figure 8 has no note at all, so a reader has only the misleading caption.
- The paper's most quotable number cannot be reproduced from the model it is attributed to. On p.12 the combined ZIP predictions are 5.35 (suburb), 3.64 (city), 2.41 (town), 1.81 (rural), yielding 'more than twice as many as town' (2.22×) and 'nearly three times as many as rural' (2.96×). Back out the implied structural-zero probabilities against the immediately preceding λ values (5.869/5.669/5.039/4.936): π = .088 suburb, .358 city, .512 town, .641 rural. Those are irreconcilable with Model B's zero-inflation coefficients, which put city, town and rural all at or BELOW suburb (−.038, −.192, −.363) at common covariates. The combined predictions must therefore be evaluated at each locale's own covariate means — including school enrollment — so they are not the size-adjusted contrast the surrounding paragraph implies. Consistent with that, they closely track the raw descriptive gap: Table 1's k=1..5 tail sums give lower-bound raw means of ~3.47 (suburb) vs ~1.50 (rural), the same ~3:1 shape.
- The p.11 topic sentence contradicts the sentence that follows it. 'City and rural-located schools have much higher odds, relative to suburban AND TOWN schools, of having no structural support' — but the reference category is suburb only, and the very next sentence says 'city, rural, and town schools have larger odds ... relative to suburban schools,' listing town at 1.9% higher. A reader has to stop and work out which comparison is meant.
- The zero-inflation latent class is repeatedly reified as an observed school attribute — 'no structural support,' 'no capacity for AP STEM courses,' 'schools with capacity to offer AP STEM coursework,' 'the probability of a school having the capacity to support AP STEM coursework.' Nothing in the data measures capacity; the ZIP mixture is a distributional device. The p.9–10 setup is careful, but the results prose treats the model output as if capacity had been observed.
- Nulls are narrated as findings without qualification. Town Calc AB (.164, SE .100) and city CS Principles (.131, SE .075) are both under two standard errors and unstarred in Table 4, yet appear on p.14 as '17.8% higher odds' and '14.0% higher odds' alongside the significant rural Calc AB result. Similarly, 'rural and town schools are still less likely to offer each AP STEM course, with the exception of AP Calculus AB' (p.14) glosses over Biology (rural −.024, town −.049, both ns and effectively zero), Chemistry (rural −.123, ns), and CS Principles (rural −.134, town −.250, both ns). Figure 9's error bars show all of this; the prose does not. The p.6 argument that significance is not meaningful for population data is a defensible stance, but it is stated once and never reconciled with the stars printed on both tables.
- The e^−.363 ÷ e^.341 = 0.495 calculation on p.11 is arithmetically correct (= e^−.704) but mis-framed. It is a ratio of two odds ratios drawn from two different models, and 'nearly halves' understates what actually happened: the rural-vs-suburban odds ratio moves from 1.41 to 0.70, i.e., it reverses sign. 'Nearly halves' invites a reader to hear a probability falling by half.
- 'AP Physics C: Magnetism, +26.58%' (p.13) should read AP Physics C: Mechanics — +26.58 is the Mechanics figure (1,383/12,780 minus 24.53%). A published typo in a sentence that names all three physics courses.
- 'The gradient fill of the choropleths is identical to that in Figure 6' (p.12) is misleading. Figure 6's legend runs to about 6 courses; Figure 7's runs to about 8. The color ramp is the same but the value domain is not, so identical colors in the two figures mean different course counts — precisely the cross-figure comparison the sentence invites.
- Figure 3 carries claims its legend cannot support. The prose describes four locale categories with inline color swatches ('over 70% have primarily rural high school populations (■), over 25% ... town-located (■)'), but the bivariate diamond legend has only a City↔Rural axis crossed with a Low↔High median axis; town and suburb have no legend position. The swatches themselves are small colored squares carrying load-bearing meaning — they vanish in grayscale, in screen readers, and in text extraction.
- Three abbreviation schemes for the same courses across adjacent exhibits: Table 3 uses 'AP CompSciA'/'AP CompScP', Table 4 uses 'COMPSCA'/'COMSCP' (note the inconsistent COMP/COM within a single header row), and Figure 9 uses 'ComSciA'/'ComSciP'. Minor, but it adds friction to exactly the cross-referencing the paper asks of readers.
- Neither Table 2 nor Table 4 states in its note what the parentheses contain; a reader must go back to p.6 to learn they are state-clustered robust standard errors. Table 2's note defines a '+ p < .1' tier that Table 4's does not, and Table 4 is set rotated 90° on p.16 despite being the paper's single most load-bearing exhibit.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not quote the abstract's 'the likelihood of offering each course' — the body's own Table 4 has AP Calculus AB going the other way (rural +28.8%, town +17.8% odds). Quote conclusion item (3) instead, which states the exception correctly.
- If you take one thing from this paper, take the school-size result, not the locale result. The abstract does not mention it. The pivot is Table 2, Model A vs Model B, zero-inflated panel: city .375→−.038, rural .341→−.363, town .019→−.192. Adjusting for enrollment reverses the sign of every locale coefficient on the probability of a structural zero.
- Do not cite 'suburban schools offer nearly three times as many STEM courses as rural schools' (p.12) as an adjusted estimate. Back-solving the four combined predictions (5.35/3.64/2.41/1.81) against the λ values in the previous paragraph implies structural-zero probabilities of .088/.358/.512/.641, which contradict Model B's own zero-inflation coefficients. These are locale-specific-covariate predictions, and they land close to the raw descriptive gap. The adjusted count-model gaps are the modest ones: 3.4% (city), 14.1% (rural), 15.9% (town).
- Read Table 1 and Table 4 directly; treat Figures 2 and 8 as decoration until you have worked out what their bars plot. Both axes say 'Percent of U.S. Public High Schools' and both plot each locale's share of the course-offering subset instead. If you want within-locale offering rates — the quantity most readers assume these figures show — they are in Table 1 and Table 3, not in the figures.
- The load-bearing exhibits are Table 1 (raw locale × course-count grid), Table 2 (the two ZIP models side by side — this is where the school-size story lives), Table 4 (twelve per-course logits), and Figure 9 (Table 4 rendered as percent change in odds with CIs). A time-constrained reader can get the whole paper from these four plus the discussion.
- Read Figure 9 alongside every per-course claim in the p.14–15 prose. Its confidence intervals disclose what the text does not: town Calc AB and city CS Principles both straddle zero, and the Biology and CS Principles rural/town coefficients are essentially nil. The text's 'rural and town schools are still less likely to offer each AP STEM course, with the exception of AP Calculus AB' is really about 8 of 12 courses.
- Treat 'structural support' and 'capacity' as model vocabulary, not measurement. Whenever the paper says a school has 'no capacity for AP STEM courses,' substitute 'is assigned to the zero-inflation component,' and the claims stay accurate.
- Before relying on 'gaps are largest for high-math-demand courses,' read footnote 10 (p.22). The definition it gives makes Calculus AB, Calculus BC, and Statistics all high-math-demand — courses whose gaps are reversed, largest, and middling respectively — while AP Computer Science A, which the largest-gap list includes, fits none of the stated criteria.
- Skimmable: the Theoretical Framing and Background section (pp.2–5) is a competent but conventional OTL and locale-inequity review that the results do not depend on. The GWLR state-by-state narration (pp.15, 18) is illustrative rather than estimated — footnote 4 says the author deliberately reports no GWLR coefficients — so Figures 10 and 11 are suggestive maps, not evidence you can quote a number from.
- Not skimmable: pp.9–10 (structural vs sampling zeros) and p.11 (Model A vs Model B). Nothing later in the paper is interpretable without them.
- Small corrections to carry with you: 'AP Physics C: Magnetism, +26.58%' on p.13 means Mechanics; and Figures 6 and 7 do NOT share a color scale despite the p.12 sentence saying the gradient fill is identical (Fig. 6 tops out near 6 courses, Fig. 7 near 8), so do not compare shades across the two maps.
- Descriptive numbers in this paper are reliable — I recomputed roughly thirty of them from Tables 1 and 3 and every one matched. The places to slow down are the modeled quantities on pp.11–12 and p.14, and the abstract.

**Detailed Commentary:**

ORGANIZATION AND NAVIGABILITY. The paper is well built for a reader who wants to skim. Every results subsection opens with a declarative italic heading that states the finding ('Number of AP STEM Course Offerings Is Disproportionately Higher in Suburban Schools and Lower in Rural Schools'; 'Joint Consideration of Locale and School Size Is Critical to Understand AP STEM Availability'; 'With Sociodemographic Controls, Low Availability Persists in Town and Rural Schools for Majority of AP STEM Subjects'), and each is followed by a topic sentence restating it. The Results section also opens (p.7) with an explicit six-part roadmap. A reader can reconstruct the argument from headings alone, which is exactly what a descriptive landscape paper of this length needs. The argument is carried by four exhibits: Table 1 (raw locale × course-count grid), Table 2 (the two ZIP specifications side by side), Table 4 (twelve per-course logits), and Figure 9 (Table 4 as percent change in odds, with CIs). Figures 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, and 11 are six full-page maps that illustrate spatial heterogeneity but yield no quotable estimate — footnote 4 says outright that GWLR coefficients are withheld. A time-constrained reader can stop after the four core exhibits plus the discussion.

TEXT-VS-TABLE FIDELITY: WHAT CHECKS OUT. I recomputed every number the prose quotes from Tables 1 and 3, and the record is close to spotless. p.7: 3,409+4,101+1,821+3,826 = 13,157 of 21,139 = 62.24%, matching 'over 62%'; suburb 79.08%, rural 48.02% match. p.8: 21,139 − 13,157 = 7,982 = 37.76%, matching '7,982 (37.8%)', and the locale breakdown 1,701+1,085+1,055+4,141 sums exactly to 7,982. Suburb 5,186/21,139 = 24.53% and rural 7,967/21,139 = 37.69% match '24.5%' and '37.7%'; the 4+ group is 2,208+3,356+860+1,677 = 8,101, of which suburb is 41.43% and rural 20.70%, matching '41.4%' and '20.7%', and the over/under-representation figures of 16.9% and 17.0% are 16.89 and −16.99. p.11: exp(.375)−1 = 45.50%, exp(.341)−1 = 40.64%, exp(.019)−1 = 1.92% — all three match. exp(−.035) = −3.44% vs '3.41%', exp(−.152) = −14.10% vs '14.14%', exp(−.173) = −15.89% vs '15.90%' (differences consistent with rounded coefficients). The expected counts are internally coherent: 5.869 × (1−.0341) = 5.669, × (1−.1414) = 5.039, × (1−.1590) = 4.936, all three as printed. p.12–13: Calc AB (2,782+3,773+1,518+3,021)/21,139 = 52.48%; Biology 44.64%; Chemistry 36.84%; Physics 2 10.17%; Physics C Mechanics 12.80%; Physics C E&M 7.42% — all six match. 'Suburban schools offer these courses at more than twice the national rates, while rural and town schools offer them at less than half' holds for all three physics courses (e.g. Physics 2: 20.42/10.17 = 2.01×; rural 4.14/10.17 = 0.41×; town 4.69/10.17 = 0.46×). All ten disproportionality figures on p.13 reproduce as share-of-offering-schools minus share-of-all-schools, to within .01. Rural shares of 27.23% (Calc AB), 25.06% (Biology), 23.27% (Chemistry) and the −10.46% and −9.40% figures are exact. p.14–15: the town coefficient ranking (E&M −.905, Calc BC −.566, Physics 2 −.466, Mechanics −.461, CS A −.448) confirms that Calculus BC is genuinely the second-largest town-suburban gap. p.19–20: 'the city-suburban gaps are the largest locale gaps within all three of the aforementioned subjects' holds — Biology city −.177 vs rural −.024 and town −.049; Calc AB city −.170 is the only negative of the three; Chemistry city −.339 vs rural −.123 and town −.162. And the discussion's top-five largest-disparity list matches a full magnitude ranking of Table 4's rural and town rows. Readers can trust this paper's descriptive arithmetic.

WHERE THE RHETORIC OUTRUNS THE RESULTS. Three places, in ascending order of consequence. First, the p.11 subsection reifies the ZIP latent class. 'No structural support for AP STEM coursework,' 'no capacity for AP STEM courses,' and 'the probability of a school having the capacity to support AP STEM coursework' all describe an unobserved mixture component as though capacity had been measured. The pp.9–10 exposition of structural vs sampling zeros is careful and honest, which makes the slippage in the results prose more noticeable. The same subsection contains a flat internal contradiction: the topic sentence says city and rural schools have higher odds 'relative to suburban and town schools,' but town is not a reference category and the next sentence lists town among the locales with higher odds than suburb. Second, the odds-ratio-of-odds-ratios calculation. e^−.363 ÷ e^.341 = e^−.704 = 0.495, so the arithmetic is right, but the sentence 'the odds ratio of having no capacity for AP STEM courses nearly halves' describes a comparison across two different models and undersells what happened: the rural-vs-suburb odds ratio goes from 1.41 to 0.70, a sign reversal, not a halving of anything a reader would naturally picture.

Third, and most consequential, the combined predictions on p.12. The paragraph opens 'Combining both the zero-inflated and count model portions to consider overall estimates,' immediately after a paragraph that explicitly holds covariates at suburban means, and reports 5.35 (suburb), 3.64 (city), 2.41 (town), 1.81 (rural), then delivers the paper's most quotable line: suburban schools offer 'more than twice as many STEM courses as town schools and nearly three times as many as rural schools' (5.35/2.41 = 2.22; 5.35/1.81 = 2.96 — both internally consistent). But these cannot be the size-adjusted contrasts. Combined = (1−π)λ. Using the λ values from the preceding paragraph, the implied π values are .088 (suburb), .358 (city), .512 (town), .641 (rural). Model B's zero-inflation locale coefficients are −.038, −.192, −.363 relative to suburb — every one at or below suburb, which would put all four π values near .088 and yield a city combined prediction near 5.19, not 3.64. The only reconciliation is that these predictions are evaluated at each locale's own covariate means, school enrollment included, so the very variable the section just showed to be decisive is allowed back in. That reading is corroborated by the descriptive data: summing Table 1's k=1..5 threshold proportions gives lower-bound raw means of ~3.47 (suburb) versus ~1.50 (rural), the same roughly 3:1 shape as 5.35 vs 1.81. So the sentence a reader is most likely to carry away from this paper is, in substance, the unadjusted gap presented at the close of the adjusted-analysis section. Nothing in the text flags the change of convention.

ABSTRACT FIDELITY. Two problems. The abstract asserts rural and town deficits in 'the likelihood of offering each course,' which the body contradicts for AP Calculus AB (rural +28.8%, town +17.8% odds after controls) and which the conclusion states correctly. And the abstract never mentions school size, despite the paper's own results heading calling it critical, the discussion calling it a critical predictor, and conclusion item (2) listing it as one of five findings. Adding enrollment flips every locale coefficient in the zero-inflation model. An abstract-only reader gets a clean locale story with the mediator removed. The abstract's second clause — 'gaps are smallest for core-adjacent STEM courses and largest for high-math-demand courses' — is half sound. The core-adjacent half checks out (Biology, Calc AB, Chemistry have the three smallest rural/town gaps in Table 4, in that order). The high-math-demand half does not survive footnote 10 (p.22), which defines the category to include courses that 'are mathematics courses themselves.' That sweeps in Calculus AB, whose gap is reversed and is the paper's stated exception; Calculus BC, whose gap is second-largest; and Statistics, which sits mid-pack (rural −.317, town −.313). Meanwhile AP Computer Science A appears in the largest-gap list without satisfying any of footnote 10's criteria. Conclusion item (4) has to carve out Calculus AB by name to keep the claim standing; the abstract carries no such caveat. The category is never enumerated anywhere in the paper, and footnote 10's syntax ('conceptualized as the AP courses, which are mathematics courses themselves, are calculus-based ... or suggest pre-calculus as a prerequisite') is hard to parse on first reading.

EXHIBITS: HONESTY AND SELF-CONTAINMENT. Figures 2 and 8 are the clearest reader traps in the paper. Both carry the x-axis label 'Percent of U.S. Public High Schools.' Neither plots that. In Figure 2's '1+' pane the city bar reads roughly 26%: not 3,409/21,139 = 16.1% (what the axis claims) and not 66.71% (what Table 1's corresponding row and the figure's own note describe), but 3,409/13,157 = 25.9% — city's share of the schools offering 1+. The same holds throughout Figure 8: the CALCAB suburb bar reads ~34% = 3,773/11,094, not 17.9% and not Table 3's 72.75%. Figure 2's note makes it worse by stating the panes show 'the proportion of schools in each locale offering 1+, 2+, 3+, 4+, and 5+ AP STEM courses' — which is the Table 1 quantity, a third thing. Figure 8 has no note whatsoever, so its caption ('Percent of U.S. Public Schools Offering Each AP STEM Course by Locale') is the reader's only guide, and it points at Table 3's numbers rather than the plotted ones. The prose, notably, interprets both figures correctly — the p.8 walk-through of the 4+ pane is exactly right — so the errors live in the labeling, not the reasoning. But a reader who goes to Figure 8 to check a Table 3 percentage will be reading a different statistic and will not be told.

Other exhibit issues. Figure 3 is a bivariate choropleth whose legend has only a City↔Rural axis crossed with a Low↔High median axis, yet the accompanying prose classifies counties into all four NCES locales and encodes them with small inline colored squares in running text ('over 25% have primarily town-located high school populations (■)'). Town and suburb have no position on that legend, and the swatches carry load-bearing meaning that disappears in grayscale, in screen readers, and in text extraction. The p.12 claim that Figure 7's gradient is 'identical to that in Figure 6' is not right in the sense that matters: the ramp is the same but the domains differ (Fig. 6 to about 6 courses, Fig. 7 to about 8), so the same shade means different counts in the two maps — exactly the comparison the sentence invites. Figure 7's Montana suburban panel is grey with no note explaining it; Figure 4's greys get footnote 7. On the positive side, Figures 5 and 9 plot 95% CIs and Figure 10's note candidly warns that its legend is not symmetric — both are more forthcoming than the prose that describes them.

TABLE APPARATUS. Neither Table 2 nor Table 4 says in its note what the parentheses contain; the reader must return to the Analytic Strategy on p.6 to learn they are state-clustered robust standard errors. Table 2's note defines a '+p < .1' tier that Table 4's does not use, a small inconsistency between adjacent exhibits. Table 4 is set rotated 90° on p.16, which is understandable for twelve columns but awkward for the paper's most-consulted exhibit. Course abbreviations differ across three exhibits — Table 3's 'AP CompSciA'/'AP CompScP', Table 4's 'COMPSCA'/'COMSCP' (inconsistent even within one header row), Figure 9's 'ComSciA'/'ComSciP' — which slows the cross-referencing the paper repeatedly asks for. Footnote 6 is attached to the Figure 3 caption and is a code-attribution credit, which interrupts the substantive footnote sequence between 5 and 7. One published typo: 'AP Physics C: Magnetism, +26.58%' (p.13) should be Mechanics — the figure is Mechanics' (1,383/12,780 − 24.53%). The 'BolesShort Title' string that appears in text extraction is in SAGE's invisible article-ID stamp layer, not on the printed page; it is an extraction artifact, not a visible production error, and readers can ignore it.

STATISTICAL REPORTING IN PROSE. The paper argues on p.6 that with population data 'significance and standard errors are not particularly useful,' then prints stars on both tables and never invokes significance in the results narration. That is at least internally consistent, but it shifts work onto the reader. Two of the paper's named exceptions rest on coefficients under two standard errors — town Calculus AB (.164, SE .100) and city CS Principles (.131, SE .075), both unstarred — and are reported on p.14 in the same sentence structure as the starred rural Calculus AB result. More broadly, 'rural and town schools are still less likely to offer each AP STEM course, with the exception of AP Calculus AB' (p.14) and the discussion's '11 of the 12 courses' both overstate: Biology's rural and town coefficients are −.024 and −.049 (both ns, effectively zero), Chemistry's rural is −.123 (ns), and CS Principles' are −.134 and −.250 (both ns). Figure 9's error bars disclose all of this; the prose does not. The realistic count is closer to eight of twelve with clear rural and town gaps.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** The "11 of the 12 courses" sentence is on p. 19, in the Discussion, not in the abstract, and the criticism of it is withdrawn. Eleven of the twelve rural and town point estimates in Table 4 are negative, and p. 6 states that significance tests and standard errors are "not particularly useful" for full-population data, so by the paper's own standard the count is right. If significance is applied anyway, eight or nine of the estimates are distinguishable from zero; that is a caveat for readers, not an error in the paper. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

DENSITY AND LENGTH. At 24 pages with six maps, the paper runs long for what it establishes, but the padding is front-loaded and skippable. The theoretical framing and background (pp.2–5) is a competent, conventional review of OTL theory and locale inequity that the results do not depend on; the p.5 research question can be reached directly. The GWLR narration (pp.15, 18) is qualitative by design and yields no citable estimate. What must not be skipped is short: pp.9–10 for the structural-vs-sampling-zero distinction, and p.11 for the Model A/Model B comparison. Nothing after p.11 is interpretable without those two pages.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

Boles uses the full population of College Board AP course-audit records (2015–2019) joined to NCES CCD/EDGE for all 21,139 U.S. public high schools to map locale disparities in AP STEM course availability, in aggregate (zero-inflated Poisson) and course-by-course (12 state-FE logits), with a geographically weighted layer showing within-state heterogeneity. The headline finding — rural and town schools offer fewer AP STEM courses — confirms a well-established pattern; the genuinely new contributions are the course-level national estimates (Table 4), the modeled treatment of the count/variety outcome, and the demonstration that locale gaps vary sharply by subject and by region. It is a careful, honest descriptive contribution to an important question, but its most quotable number ('suburban schools offer nearly three times as many AP STEM courses as rural schools') is not the number its adjusted models support.

**Strengths:**

- Genuinely new data application: the College Board AP audit file at the school level, nationally, for the full population of public high schools (N = 21,139, p. 5). Prior comparable work was either district-level (Gagnon & Mattingly, 2016) or restricted to AP-program/AP-STEM presence in aggregate (Handwerk et al., 2008; S. Mann et al., 2017). Table 3 (~p. 14) and Table 4 (~p. 16) provide, so far as I can tell, the first national course-by-course availability estimates for all 12 AP STEM subjects with school-level covariates and state fixed effects. That table is the paper's durable asset.
- The subject-level disaggregation produces findings that are not simply 'rural schools offer less,' and are the most interesting thing in the paper: AP Calculus AB reverses sign under controls (rural +28.8%, town +17.8% odds relative to suburb, Table 4/Figure 9), city schools lead on AP Computer Science Principles (+14.0%) and AP Environmental Science (+21.1%), and the largest deficits concentrate in AP Physics C: E&M, Physics C: Mechanics, Physics 2, Calculus BC, and CS A. The 'depth in rural/town, breadth in cities' reading (~p. 20) is a genuinely useful reframing of an old finding.
- Population data rather than a sample, with the author explicitly noting that inference is not really the point (p. 6) — a rare and appropriate piece of statistical honesty, even if stars are still reported to field norms.
- The spatial layer (Figures 4, 7, 10, 11) does real work rather than decorating. The Northeast rural exception (rural schools in CT, DE, MD, MA, NJ with median 4+ AP STEM courses vs. rural median of zero in 23 states, ~p. 9) and the within-New York divergence between Physics C: E&M and Calculus BC gaps establish that 'rural' is not a single condition. This complements Drescher et al. (2022) and the author's companion outcome paper.
- The limitations section (~pp. 20–21) is unusually forthright: audit ≠ enrollment; AP is not the only advanced pathway; NCES locale codes are coarse and treat a wealthy rural destination community like an isolated distressed farming community. The paper draws its own boundaries honestly, which materially raises how much a reader can trust it.
- The zero-inflated specification is a good fit to the substantive problem — separating schools that structurally cannot support any AP STEM program from schools that could but did not offer a given course — and the school-size result within it is the paper's strongest single analytic finding.

**Weaknesses:**

- The most quotable claim is the least well-supported. 'Suburban schools offer more than twice as many STEM courses as town schools and nearly three times as many as rural schools' (~p. 12; 5.35 vs. 2.41 vs. 1.81) is presented immediately after the adjusted count-model contrasts and reads as a covariate-adjusted result. It cannot be. Under Model B, rural schools conditional on size have LOWER odds of a structural zero than suburban schools (coefficient −0.363, OR 0.70), and the count multiplier is exp(−0.152) = 0.86; holding covariates at suburban means, the combined rural prediction would be at or above the suburban value, not a third of it. The 5.35/1.81 pair must be fitted values at each locale's own observed covariates — i.e., a restatement of the raw distribution in Table 1 (79.1% vs. 48.0% offering 1+), not a ceteris paribus contrast. The paper never says which, and the '3x' figure is the one destined to be cited.
- The estimand question the paper does not confront: if smallness IS rurality, what does 'controlling for school size' identify? Model B's zero-inflated component says a rural school and a suburban school of the same enrollment are similarly or more likely to support AP STEM — an interesting mechanism finding, but not a policy-relevant contrast, since the rural school cannot choose to have 1,800 students. The paper reports the size-adjusted estimates as if they strip out confounding when they arguably condition on a mediator that is constitutive of the treatment. Readers should treat 'school size accounts for much of the locale gap' as a decomposition, not an explanation that dissolves the disparity.
- The 'structural zero' vs. 'sampling zero' distinction (~p. 10) is a mixture-model artifact given a substantive label. Nothing in the data identifies which schools lack an AP program versus rely on IB/DE; the assignment is entirely model-driven. The claim that city and rural schools have 'no structural support for AP STEM coursework' should be read as a statement about a latent class in a ZIP, not a measured institutional fact.
- The measure is 'ever authorized to use the AP label in any of four years,' which is neither point-in-time availability nor courses actually taught nor enrollment. The paper says so, but only in limitations. The four-year union inflates availability everywhere, and probably inflates it most for schools with intermittent offerings — plausibly small/rural schools — which would make the reported rural gaps a conservative lower bound on any single-year gap. That is a favorable direction, but it is an inference the paper does not make and does not test.
- Data vintage undercuts the course-level rankings. AP Computer Science Principles launched in 2016–17, so its low rural numbers partly reflect rollout timing rather than a steady-state disparity; AP Precalculus (added 2023) is absent entirely; the CSforAll push, state CS mandates, and post-2020 virtual AP delivery all fall outside the window. A 2026 publication reporting 2015–2019 course-specific availability is a historical baseline, not a current picture, and the paper does not flag this vintage risk as a limitation.
- The disproportionality metric (Figure 8, ~p. 15) is mechanically bounded by each locale's share of all schools — footnote 11 concedes town underrepresentation can never exceed 13.61%. Comparing a −23.09% rural figure to a −9.40% town figure is therefore not comparing like with like, yet the text ranks them against each other (~p. 15).
- The policy discussion runs ahead of the evidence in two places. The critique of online delivery (~p. 19) rests entirely on cited COVID-era literature, not on anything in these data — and sits in tension with the paper's own footnote 2, which implies that AP taken through an external virtual provider is credited to whichever school of record completes the audit, so the measure may misattribute exactly the delivery model being discussed. The call for 'targeted efforts' in rural and town schools follows from the descriptive gaps but is not informed by any evaluation of the mechanisms the paper speculates about (teacher supply, PD, local demand).
- GWLR estimates are shown as maps only, with model estimates withheld for multicollinearity and sparseness reasons (footnote 4), and no bandwidth, fit statistics, or uncertainty surface is reported. The spatial layer is therefore evocative and directional but not an inferential result a reader can build on.
- Data are under a restricted DUA and cannot be shared (~p. 21), so the population-level tables that constitute the paper's main contribution are not directly reproducible; a data access guide is provided instead.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the first national, school-level, course-by-course description of AP STEM availability by NCES locale for the full population of U.S. public high schools, 2015–2019. Table 3 (unadjusted shares) and Table 4 (state-FE logits with school-size and sociodemographic controls) are the reference exhibits.
- CITE IT FOR: the finding that locale gaps are subject-specific, not uniform — smallest (and reversed for AP Calculus AB) in core-adjacent courses, largest in high-math-demand courses (Physics C: E&M and Mechanics, Physics 2, Calculus BC, CS A). This is the paper's most defensible novel claim and holds in both adjusted and unadjusted analyses.
- CITE IT FOR: the demonstration that rurality has heterogeneous curricular implications by region — Northeast rural schools resemble suburban ones on AP STEM breadth while rural schools in 23 states have a county median of zero (Figures 4, 7). Good supporting evidence for arguments that NCES locale codes are too coarse.
- CITE IT FOR: school enrollment as the dominant school-level correlate of whether a school supports any AP STEM program at all (Table 2, Model B), including that adding size flips the sign on all three locale coefficients in the zero-inflated component.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: 'suburban schools offer nearly three times as many AP STEM courses as rural schools, controlling for school characteristics.' The 5.35 vs. 1.81 comparison is inconsistent with the paper's own Model B coefficients as an adjusted contrast and is effectively a restatement of the raw locale distribution — quote Table 1 directly instead if you want the descriptive gap.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: how many AP STEM courses a school actually offered or taught in a given year. The measure is authorization to use the AP label at any point across four years; it overstates point-in-time availability by construction.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: student access, enrollment, participation, or outcomes. Availability is explicitly framed as necessary but insufficient; accessibility is treated in the companion paper (Boles & Domingue, 2023).
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: causal claims about locale or about what would happen if rural schools were larger. All estimates are descriptive associations on population data with state fixed effects and no design for identification.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: current computer science availability disparities. AP CSP was in its first years during the study window, so its rural deficit conflates rollout timing with steady-state inequity.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: total advanced STEM opportunity. IB, AICE, dual enrollment, and locally designed advanced courses are excluded, and DE in particular has conflicting locale findings in the literature (Spencer & Maldonado, 2021 vs. Gagnon et al., 2021) — a rural school with strong DE is coded as a zero here.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: precise localized gap magnitudes from the GWLR maps (Figures 10, 11). Estimates are deliberately unreported and should be read as directional patterns only.
- OPEN QUESTION for readers: whether the size-adjusted locale estimates are the policy-relevant quantity at all, given that small enrollment is partly constitutive of rurality rather than a confounder of it. The unadjusted gaps (Table 1, Table 3) may be the better guide for resource allocation.
- OPEN QUESTION: whether these patterns hold after 2019 — post-pandemic virtual AP delivery, state AP mandates, CS education legislation, and AP Precalculus all postdate the data. Treat this as a 2015–2019 baseline against which to measure change.
- OPEN QUESTION: whether audit authorization tracks courses actually taught, and whether the audit-to-enrollment gap itself varies by locale. If small rural schools authorize courses they cannot consistently staff, the true availability gap is larger than reported.
- WHAT IT SETS UP: the companion exam-results paper (Boles & Domingue, 2023) on accessibility and success; development of finer-grained rurality measures beyond population size, density, and distance; and evaluation of the state policy levers the paper names (AP offering mandates, fee waivers, AdvanceKentucky, state virtual initiatives).

**Detailed Commentary:**

**What is actually new.** The claim that rural and small schools offer fewer AP courses is one of the better-established regularities in the rural education literature, running from Monk and Haller (1993) through Handwerk et al. (2008), Iatarola et al. (2011), Gagnon and Mattingly (2015, 2016), and S. Mann et al. (2017). The paper is candid about this — it positions itself as extending Mann et al. from 'has any AP STEM course' to 'how many and which ones' (~p. 18). Judged against that framing, three things here are genuinely new. First, the data asset: the College Board audit file gives every school–course authorization pair for the population, which is finer than CRDC-derived and district-level sources and finer than the survey-based work it extends. Second, the course-level estimates in Table 4 (~p. 16) — twelve separate state-FE logits with school size, IPR, and racial composition controls — for which I am aware of no prior national equivalent. Third, the GWLR layer, which demonstrates that locale gaps are not a national constant but vary within states (the New York contrast between Figures 10 and 11 is the sharpest illustration: town schools in the NYC metro out-offer suburban peers in Physics C: E&M, while in the Finger Lakes and Southern Tier the town advantage appears in Calculus BC instead).

The rest largely confirms. That is not a criticism of the paper's honesty — it says as much — but it does bound how much a reader should update. If you already believed rural schools have thinner advanced STEM offerings, this paper gives you a much better-resolved picture of that belief rather than a reason to revise it.

**The quotable-versus-supported gap.** This is the issue a reader most needs to know about. In the count-model section (~pp. 11–12), the author correctly presents ceteris paribus predictions holding covariates at suburban means: 5.869 courses for suburban schools, 5.669 city, 5.039 rural, 4.936 town — differences of roughly one course, which matches exp(−0.152) applied to 5.869. Immediately after, the text combines the zero-inflated and count components and reports 5.35 suburban, 3.64 city, 2.41 town, 1.81 rural, concluding that 'suburban schools offer more than twice as many STEM courses as town schools and nearly three times as many as rural schools.' That sentence is the one that will be quoted, and it is not an adjusted contrast. Under Model B the rural zero-inflation coefficient is −0.363, meaning that conditional on enrollment and sociodemographics, rural schools are about 30% LESS likely than suburban schools to be structural zeros. Feeding suburban-mean covariates through both components would push the rural combined prediction toward or above the suburban one, not down to 1.81. The 5.35/1.81 pair can only be arriving from each school's own observed covariates — that is, it is a fitted reproduction of the raw distribution already in Table 1 (79.1% of suburban vs. 48.0% of rural schools offering 1+ AP STEM course). Presenting it inside the adjusted-analysis section, with 'with school sociodemographic and enrollment controls' in the same sentence, invites exactly the misreading that the 3x gap survives adjustment. It does not; the paper's own Model B says the opposite about the extensive margin. A reader who wants the descriptive gap should cite Table 1; a reader who wants the adjusted gap should cite the ~1-course count-model difference and the Table 4 course-level odds.

**Is 'controlling for size' the right estimand?** The paper's second-most-quotable claim — school size 'accounts for much of the relationship between geographic locale and structural support for AP STEM coursework' (~p. 11) — is a real and well-executed descriptive decomposition, and the sign flip on all three locale dummies between Models A and B is a clean, informative result. But the paper does not engage with what the adjusted coefficient means. Rural schools are small in substantial part because they are rural; enrollment is closer to a mediator or a component of the treatment than a confounder. Conditioning on it answers 'do rural schools underperform other schools of the same size?' (answer: no, and on the extensive margin they do somewhat better), which is a useful mechanism finding but is not the question a policymaker deciding whether to invest in rural AP STEM is asking. The paper's own discussion (~pp. 18–19) treats the finding both ways at once — as evidence that size explains the gap and as motivation for rural-targeted investment — without reconciling them. Readers should hold both facts simultaneously: rural students face a large unconditional deficit, and that deficit operates substantially through school scale, which limits the set of remedies that could plausibly close it.

**Measurement bounds on the contribution.** The outcome is 'was this school ever authorized to label a course AP in any of 2015–16 through 2018–19.' Three distinct slippages follow: authorization is not offering, offering is not enrollment, and a four-year union is not a year. The author names all three (~p. 20) and correctly says audit data overstate availability. What she does not do is reason about the direction of bias in the locale comparison. My read is that the four-year collapse should inflate availability more for schools whose offerings are intermittent — plausibly the small and rural schools that cannot staff a course every year — which would make the reported rural gaps conservative relative to any single-year measure. If that is right, it strengthens the paper's substantive conclusion, and it is a shame the point is left on the table. Footnote 2 raises a separate wrinkle that matters more than its placement suggests: a school of record must complete the audit to list AP on a transcript even for a course taken online. This means externally delivered AP that a rural student takes through a state virtual school may or may not appear against her home school, depending on transcript arrangements — which is uncomfortable, since online delivery is precisely the policy channel the discussion (~p. 19) evaluates.

**Vintage.** A 2026 article reporting 2015–2019 availability faces an obvious relevance question that the limitations section never raises. AP Computer Science Principles debuted in 2016–17, so its large rural deficit in Table 3 and Figure 9 partly measures rollout, not equilibrium — a specific caution for anyone citing this in the CS-for-All literature. AP Precalculus, now among the most consequential AP STEM courses for exactly the marginal schools this paper studies, did not exist. And the pandemic-era expansion of virtual AP, state AP mandates, and CS legislation all fall outside the window. The right way to cite this is as a well-documented pre-pandemic baseline.

**Standing in the literature.** With the caveats above, this is now the best available single source on school-level, course-specific AP STEM availability by locale nationally. It supersedes district-level and aggregate-presence work on granularity and coverage, and its course-by-course table is the kind of exhibit that gets reused. It does not supersede anything on access, enrollment, or outcomes, and it makes no causal claims. What it sets up is clear and the author states it: the companion accessibility paper using exam data (Boles & Domingue, 2023), development of rurality measures finer than population/density/distance, and evaluation of the state policy levers named at the end (~p. 21) — offering mandates, fee waivers, AdvanceKentucky, state online initiatives. The most valuable follow-on the paper implies but does not name is a comparison of audit records to actual course enrollment or staffing, which would put an empirical bound on the availability–offering gap this paper's measure cannot see.

**Actionable knowledge beyond 'rural schools offer less.'** Three things. (1) Targeting should be course-specific: the binding constraint is not AP STEM generally but calculus-based physics, Calculus BC, and CS A, which suggests teacher content expertise and math-pipeline depth rather than AP program adoption per se. (2) Targeting should be region-specific: the Northeast rural result shows the rural deficit is not inevitable, and states are a meaningful policy unit (the state fixed effects and the within-state GWLR variation both point this way). (3) The AP Calculus AB reversal implies rural schools that do run AP STEM are running it as depth in the core sequence rather than breadth — so a breadth-oriented intervention may be pushing against the local rationale for the program, and interventions should probably build outward from the courses rural schools already sustain. None of these are demonstrated mechanisms; all three are reasonable readings of well-executed description, which is a fair summary of the paper's contribution as a whole.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

Boles reports her three data sources, her software environment down to package versions, and her two headline model specifications in full — and the printed tables are complete enough that essentially every descriptive and derived number in the prose can be checked with a calculator, which I verified. But there is no code deposit anywhere, no descriptive statistics for any covariate, no documentation of the AP-audit-to-NCES crosswalk or the CCD filters that produce N = 21,139, and the geographically weighted results behind one of the five headline findings are withheld entirely. The paper is fully auditable as a set of reported numbers and largely unreproducible as an analysis.

**Strengths:**

- The Open Practices statement (p. 21) is specific rather than boilerplate: it names the restriction (a College Board Data Use Agreement), states plainly that the data cannot be shared, and deposits a data access guide at a citable openICPSR DOI (10.3886/E247327V2). For restricted commercial data this is a real access pathway, not a gesture, and it is better than the 'available upon request' formulation still common in the field.
- The software environment is reported at a level most education papers do not reach: R 4.3.2, pscl 1.5.9, spgwr 0.6-36, and the base stats package, each with a formal citation (pp. 6-7). Even the source of adapted plotting code is credited (footnote 6).
- Both headline specifications are written out as equations (p. 6), with the reference category (suburban) named, state fixed effects shown explicitly, and the text stating unambiguously that the ZIP uses the same covariates in the zero-inflated and count components with the coefficients 'estimated separately for each component.' There is no guesswork about what is on the right-hand side.
- Results reporting in Tables 2 and 4 is generous by field standards: every coefficient with its standard error, N, AIC and BIC for both ZIP models, and AIC, BIC and Brier scores for all twelve logits. The fit statistics double as a reproducibility anchor — a replicator who rebuilds the file can compare AIC = 71,730 (Model B) or 18,050 (BIOL) against their own fit as a diagnostic before ever looking at coefficients.
- Tables 1 and 3 report raw counts alongside percentages for every locale and every threshold/course. This makes the entire unadjusted claim structure independently checkable with no data access at all — I confirmed it (see detail).
- Every derived quantity reported in the prose that comes from the regression tables is arithmetically recoverable from those tables, and each one I checked is correct: the 45.5%/40.6%/1.9% zero-inflation odds, the near-halving of the rural odds ratio (e^-.363/e^.341 = .495), the 3.41%/14.14%/15.90% expected-count changes in Figure 5, and the 28.8%/17.8%/14.0%/21.1% odds changes in Figure 9.

**Weaknesses:**

- No replication code exists in any form — not deposited, not promised on request, not described. The openICPSR deposit is characterized solely as a 'data access guide detailing the processes for data request/access' (p. 21); on the paper's own description it contains no code, no analytic-file codebook, and no variable-construction documentation.
- The single most consequential data step is entirely undocumented: how College Board AP audit school identifiers were matched to NCES school IDs. The audit file carries school names, addresses, and College Board AI codes, not NCES IDs. No crosswalk method, no match rate, and no treatment of unmatched audit records is reported. Because unmatched offering schools would be absorbed into the 21,139 as zeros, this step bears directly on the zero-inflation results that anchor the school-size finding.
- The N = 21,139 universe is asserted, never defined. 'All U.S. public high schools that did not offer AP coursework were added' (p. 5) does not say which CCD file, which school-type codes (regular/special-ed/vocational/alternative), which operational-status codes, or how charters, virtual schools, BIE/DoDEA schools, and outlying areas were handled. 'Schools offering courses for 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th-grade students' does not say whether the filter is a grade-span field or nonzero G09-G12 membership — choices that differ by hundreds of schools.
- N is identical (21,139) across both ZIP models and all twelve logits, which requires complete data on locale, IPR, enrollment, and three race proportions for every school in the frame. EDGE IPR and CCD membership are not complete in practice. The paper never states whether cases were listwise-deleted, imputed, or zero-filled, and reports no missingness diagnostics. Either the analytic sample is a complete-case subset — in which case the 'complete population' framing is overstated and the restriction undocumented — or missing values were filled in a way that is invisible.
- 'Constants were added prior to log transformation' (p. 6) names no constant. The race proportions are frequently exactly zero and IPR has a floor of 0, so offsets are unavoidable — but the choice (+.001 vs +.01 vs +1) materially changes the log-covariate coefficients. The paper also never states whether proportions are on a 0-1 or 0-100 scale, nor whether the enrollment and proportion denominators are total school membership or grades 9-12 only. Two replicators with identical data would produce different Table 2 and Table 4 numbers.
- The NCES sources are cited only as 'U.S. Department of Education (2023a/2023b)' with a bare https://nces.ed.gov/ URL. No file names, no ACS vintage for the EDGE income-to-poverty ratio, no locale-file year, no download date. CCD files are revised and EDGE IPR and locale assignments differ across vintages, so 'the NCES data' is not a single identifiable object here.
- Footnote 3 substitutes 2017-18 data for 11 schools and 2016-17 for one when 'NCES school data quality was poor in succeeding years.' The quality criterion is undefined and the schools are not listed. Small in effect but emblematic of the undocumented judgment calls throughout.
- The four audit years are collapsed to ever-offered, while covariates come from a single year (2018-19). No account is given of schools that closed during 2015-19 (no 2018-19 CCD record) or opened mid-window (fewer years of exposure to be observed offering a course) — an asymmetry that pushes toward the zero category.
- GWLR is effectively a black box. Footnote 4 declines to report estimates, citing multicollinearity and local sparseness. Beyond the estimates, the bandwidth value, kernel, adaptive-bandwidth selection criterion (CV vs AICc), distance metric, and the effective N after the Alaska/Hawaii omission (footnote 12) are all unreported. Figures 10 and 11 carry no numeric legend range in the text ('the legend is not symmetric'), so the entire fifth headline finding — that locale gaps vary within and across states — rests on quantities the reader can neither see nor bound.
- There is no descriptive statistics table for any covariate. Not one mean, SD, or range for IPR, enrollment, or the race proportions appears anywhere in the paper. This is why the predicted counts (5.869; 5.35/3.64/2.41/1.81) cannot be regenerated from Table 2 — they require the suburban covariate means, which are not reported, plus a state-fixed-effect convention that is never stated.
- The model-selection claim that ZIP 'was supported by AIC and BIC values relative to other count models considered' (p. 6) names neither the competing models (Poisson? NB? ZINB? hurdle?) nor their fit statistics. It is an unverifiable assertion.
- Cluster-robust standard errors at the state level are announced only in the RQ1a subsection (p. 6). Whether the twelve logits in Table 4 also use state-clustered SEs is never stated, and no package capable of producing a clustered sandwich for a pscl ZIP fit (sandwich, lmtest) appears in the software list.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat Tables 1 and 3 as the verifiable core of the paper and check them yourself — the arithmetic closes exactly. The locale counts sum to N (5,110 + 5,186 + 2,876 + 7,967 = 21,139); the 7,982 zero-offering schools are exactly N minus the 13,157 offering 1+, and the per-locale zeros (1,701/1,085/1,055/4,141) reconcile. Every disproportionality figure in the text is recoverable: suburban schools are 3,356/8,101 = 41.4% of schools offering 4+ against a 24.53% population share, giving the reported +16.9. Figures 2 and 8 are fully regenerable from the printed tables with no data access whatsoever. Lean on these numbers with confidence.
- Likewise verify the reported effect magnitudes rather than taking them on trust — they check out. Every percent-change in Figures 5 and 9 and in the prose is exp(coefficient) - 1 applied to Tables 2 and 4, and each one I recomputed matches. If you are citing a magnitude from this paper, recompute it from the table; you will get the same answer, and you will also see the standard error attached to it.
- Do NOT treat the predicted course counts (suburban 5.35, city 3.64, town 2.41, rural 1.81; and the count-model-only 5.869) as checkable. They depend on covariate means that appear nowhere in the paper and on an unstated convention for the state fixed effects. Cite them as the author's model-based predictions, not as quantities you have verified. If these numbers matter to your argument, request the covariate means and the prediction code from the author.
- Treat the fifth headline finding — spatial/within-state variation in locale gaps (Figures 10-11, and the Iowa, South Carolina, New York, Vermont, and Maine claims on pp. 15 and 18) — as unverifiable as reported. Footnote 4's stated reason for withholding the GWLR estimates (multicollinearity and local data sparseness) is a legitimate methodological caution, but it cuts both ways: if the local estimates are too unstable to print, the map-based regional claims inherit that instability, and the reader is given no uncertainty, no bandwidth, and no numeric range with which to judge. Read these as hypothesis-generating cartography, not as estimated gaps.
- Before relying on the adjusted regression results, ask the author for four things specifically: (1) the AP-audit-to-NCES crosswalk method and its match rate, including how unmatched audit records were treated; (2) the exact CCD/EDGE file names, years, and ACS vintage, plus the school-type, status, charter/virtual, and grade-span filters that yield N = 21,139; (3) the numeric constants added before each log transformation and the scale of the proportion variables; and (4) the missing-data rule that produces an identical N across all fourteen models. Items (1) and (4) are the two that could most plausibly move the results, since both operate directly on which schools land in the zero category.
- The openICPSR deposit (10.3886/E247327V2) is described as an access guide only. Before planning a replication, check whether it in fact contains any code or codebook — the paper's own language suggests it does not, and a replicator should budget for reconstructing the entire pipeline from scratch after obtaining the College Board data under a Data Use Agreement.
- The student-weighted version of Figure 2 is asserted on p. 8 to show that 'the relationships, while less pronounced, hold,' but lives in supplementary materials with no link or DOI given in the text. If the school-versus-student unit of analysis matters for your use — and for an equity argument about how many children are affected, it does — locate that supplement rather than accepting the one-line characterization.
- Note a small labeling error when tracing numbers: the p. 13 list of suburban overrepresentation reads 'AP Physics C: Magnetism, +26.58%.' The intended course is AP Physics C: Mechanics (1,383/2,706 = 51.11%, minus the 24.53% suburban share = 26.58%). Harmless, but it will briefly confuse anyone reconciling the text against Table 3.
- For a partial replication that avoids the restricted-data bottleneck entirely: the NCES side of this analysis (CCD membership, EDGE locale, IPR, lat/long) is fully public. A reader can independently rebuild the denominator — the count and locale distribution of U.S. public high schools — and check whether any defensible set of filters reproduces 5,110/5,186/2,876/7,967. If the locale marginals replicate under transparent filters, the sample-construction concerns above shrink considerably. The College Board audit data are the only genuine bottleneck.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This paper sits in a common and instructive position: it is highly auditable but not reproducible. Those are different properties, and readers should hold them apart when deciding how much weight to place on which findings.

On data availability, the Open Practices statement (p. 21) does the right things within a real constraint. The College Board AP course audit data are restricted under a Data Use Agreement, the statement says so plainly rather than hedging, and it points to a deposited access guide at an openICPSR DOI. That is a followable pathway in principle. What it is not is a replication package: on the paper's own description the deposit contains request/access procedures, nothing more — no code, no analytic-file codebook, no variable derivation notes. The acknowledgment carries the standard College Board attribution and disclaimer. The two public sources fare worse than the restricted one in a specific way: the NCES CCD and EDGE citations (U.S. Department of Education, 2023a, 2023b) give only a bare nces.ed.gov URL, with no file names, no release version, no download date, and — most consequentially — no ACS vintage for the EDGE income-to-poverty ratio and no year for the locale assignment file. IPR values and locale codes are not stable across EDGE releases, and log(IPR) is a covariate in all fourteen models. A replicator working from these citations alone would be guessing at the exact vintage of a variable that appears on the right-hand side of every specification in the paper.

Sample construction is where a replication would fail, and it would fail early. The frame is asserted in a single sentence on p. 5: 'all U.S. public high schools that did not offer AP coursework were added to the dataset, resulting in a total population of N = 21,139.' Every operational decision behind that sentence is invisible. Which CCD school-type codes were kept — regular only, or also special education, vocational, and alternative schools? Which operational-status codes? Charters, virtual schools, BIE and DoDEA schools, Puerto Rico and the outlying areas? The Measures section says the analysis is 'limited to schools offering courses for 9th, 10th, 11th, or 12th-grade students,' which could mean a grade-span field or nonzero G09-G12 membership; those two rules differ by hundreds of schools nationally. And notice a quiet implication of Table 1: the four locale counts sum exactly to 21,139, so every school in the frame has a non-missing locale code — which is itself the product of a filter or a fill that goes unmentioned.

More serious still is the join. The College Board audit file identifies schools by name, address, and College Board AI code, not by NCES ID. Linking it to CCD and EDGE requires a crosswalk, and the paper describes none — no matching method, no match rate, no accounting for audit records that failed to match. This is not a pedantic concern. An offering school that failed to match would be indistinguishable, in the assembled file, from a school that offered nothing, and would be counted among the 7,982 zeros. Since the paper's second headline finding is precisely about the structure of those zeros and how school size explains them (Table 2, Model A versus Model B), the undocumented step and the load-bearing result coincide. Compounding this, the four audit years are collapsed to ever-offered while covariates are drawn from 2018-19 alone (footnote 3), with no discussion of schools that closed mid-window and therefore have no 2018-19 CCD record, or that opened late and had fewer years in which to be observed offering a course. Footnote 3's substitutions for twelve schools 'when NCES school data quality was poor in succeeding years' names no quality criterion and lists no schools — small in effect, but a fair illustration of the density of undocumented judgment calls.

The constant N of 21,139 across both ZIP models and all twelve logits deserves particular scrutiny, because it is the kind of internal fact that quietly reveals an undisclosed decision. Complete data on locale, IPR, total enrollment, and three race proportions for every school in the frame is not what EDGE and CCD actually deliver; IPR in particular is missing or suppressed for a nontrivial set of schools. Yet no missing-data rule is stated, no imputation described, no listwise deletion acknowledged, and no missingness table appears. Either the analytic sample is a complete-case subset — in which case the 'complete population' framing throughout the paper is overstated and the restriction is undocumented — or missingness was handled in some way the reader cannot see. A replicator would have to guess, and the guess would change N.

Variable construction has a second, sharper irreproducibility. 'Constants were added prior to log transformation' (p. 6) is the whole of what is said about offsets. Proportions of Black, Latinx, and Asian students are frequently exactly zero in this population, and IPR has a documented floor of 0, so offsets are mandatory — but the magnitude of the offset directly determines the coefficients on those variables. Whether proportions run 0-1 or 0-100 is also never stated, which shifts both intercepts and the interpretation of the log coefficients. Nor is it stated whether 'School Enrollment' and the proportion denominators use total school membership or grades 9-12 only; the Measures section describes summing grade-by-gender-by-race counts to 'yield total school enrollment,' which suggests all grades, but many CCD high schools contain lower grades. Two honest replicators with identical raw data would produce different numbers in Tables 2 and 4. By contrast, the collapse of the twelve two-digit NCES locale codes to four primary categories is fully documented and unambiguous, as is the suburban reference category — credit where due.

Specification transparency is genuinely good for the ZIP and the logits. The equations on p. 6 are explicit, and the text resolves the question a careful reader would ask of any zero-inflated model: the same covariates enter both linear predictors, state fixed effects enter both, and the coefficients are 'estimated separately for each component.' Model A drops sqrt(enrollment) and Model B includes it, exactly as Table 2 shows. Two gaps remain. First, cluster-robust standard errors at the state level are announced only in the RQ1a subsection; whether Table 4's twelve logits share that treatment is never said, and no package that could produce a clustered sandwich for a pscl ZIP fit (sandwich, lmtest) appears among the cited software. Second, the claim that ZIP was 'supported by AIC and BIC values relative to other count models considered' names none of the alternatives and reports none of their statistics — negative binomial, ZINB, and hurdle specifications are the obvious comparisons in a paper that leans on a structural-zero interpretation, and their absence makes the modeling choice a matter of trust.

GWLR is the paper's transparency floor. Footnote 4 declines to report the estimates at all, on the stated grounds of multicollinearity and local data sparseness. That caution is defensible and even commendable in isolation, but its consequence deserves to be named: it also removes the reader's ability to judge the claims those estimates support. Beyond the coefficients, the bandwidth value is not reported, nor the kernel, nor whether the adaptive bandwidth was selected by cross-validation or AICc, nor the distance metric, nor the effective N after Alaska and Hawaii are dropped (footnote 12). Figures 10 and 11 are given no numeric legend range in the text, only the note that the scale is asymmetric. So the specific regional assertions on pp. 15 and 18 — Iowa and South Carolina showing uniform but oppositely signed town-suburban gaps in AP Physics C: E&M, New York exhibiting the largest within-state variation in both courses, Vermont and Maine the least in Calculus BC — are, for the reader, unfalsifiable. This is the one headline finding of five that a reader cannot check even in principle.

The county-level maps sit in between. Footnote 5's rule for the modal locale (largest high school student population among the four primary locales within a county) and footnote 7's graying of counties without a rural high school are clear enough to follow. What is missing is how schools were assigned to counties (CCD county FIPS, or a spatial join from EDGE lat/long?) and the boundary vintage. Figures 6 and 7 carry a different ambiguity: they map 'the mean predicted AP STEM course count from Model B,' but the paper elsewhere reports two distinct predicted quantities — a count-component-only value (5.869 for suburban schools, with footnote 8 explicitly restricting that analysis to the conditional portion) and a combined value incorporating zero inflation (5.35). Which one the choropleths display is not stated, and the two differ substantially.

What is left, then, is a paper whose descriptive spine is exceptionally checkable and whose adjusted results are inspectable but not reproducible. I verified the former directly. Table 1 is internally airtight: the locale counts sum to 21,139; 13,157 schools offer 1+ courses, leaving exactly the 7,982 zeros reported on p. 9, and the per-locale zeros reconcile school by school. The Figure 2 disproportionalities fall straight out of Table 1 — suburban schools are 3,356 of the 8,101 schools offering 4+ courses, 41.4%, against a 24.53% share of all schools, giving the +16.9 the text reports; rural schools give -17.0 the same way. Figure 8 falls out of Table 3 identically: rural schools are 3,021 of 11,094 AP Calculus AB schools, 27.23%, exactly as stated, for a -10.46 gap; suburban schools are 846 of 1,569 AP Physics C: E&M schools, 53.92%, for the reported +29.39. Every national offering rate quoted on pp. 12-13 (52.5% Calculus AB, 44.6% Biology, 36.8% Chemistry, 10.2% Physics 2, 12.8% Physics C: Mechanics, 7.4% Physics C: E&M) recomputes correctly from Table 3. And every transformed regression quantity in the prose is recoverable from Tables 2 and 4: the 45.5%, 40.6%, and 1.9% zero-inflation odds increases; the near-halving of the rural odds ratio, e^(-.363)/e^(.341) = .495 as printed; the -3.41%, -14.14%, and -15.90% expected-count changes in Figure 5; and the 28.8%, 17.8%, 14.0%, and 21.1% odds changes highlighted from Figure 9. That level of internal consistency is not universal and should raise a reader's confidence that the reported numbers are the numbers the models produced.

The conspicuous exception is the set of predicted counts. Because the paper contains no descriptive statistics table for any covariate — not a single mean, SD, or range for IPR, enrollment, or the race proportions — the statement that predictions were made 'using the suburban means of the covariates' cannot be acted on. Add the unstated convention for the state fixed effects, which alone shifts the predicted level materially, and the four numbers that carry the paper's most quotable claim (suburban schools offer more than twice as many AP STEM courses as town schools and nearly three times as many as rural schools) are the least verifiable numbers in the paper. A reader can verify that rural schools offer about 14% fewer courses conditional on having a program; a reader cannot verify the 1.81-versus-5.35 comparison.

On balance this is adequate rather than strong or weak. Adequate because the restricted-data constraint is real and honestly handled, the access pathway is deposited, the software environment is fully specified, the tables are complete with uncertainty and fit statistics, and four of five headline findings can be traced arithmetically to printed exhibits. Not strong because no code exists in any form, because a replicator with the College Board data in hand still could not rebuild the analytic file — the crosswalk, the CCD filters, the log offsets, and the missing-data rule are each individually blocking — and because one headline finding rests entirely on withheld estimates. Not weak because nothing here prevents a reader from understanding what was done or from auditing the great majority of what was claimed.
